He said, may He be exalted: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth. He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night, and He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term. Unquestionably, He is the Mighty, the Ever-Forgiving.﴾ ﴿He created you from a single soul, then made from it its mate, and He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock. He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation, in three darknesses. That is God, your Lord; to Him belongs the dominion. There is no god but Him, so how are you turned away?﴾ ﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed God is free of need of you, and He does not approve disbelief for His servants. But if you are thankful, He approves it for you. No bearer of burdens bears the burden of another. Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you of what you used to do. Indeed, He is Knower of what is in the breasts.﴾

Know that the preceding verse indicated that He, exalted, demonstrated His being free of offspring through His being one God and a Subduer, dominant, that is, of perfect power. When He established that matter upon these principles, He mentioned after it what indicates perfect power and perfect self-sufficiency. Also, He, exalted, criticized the divinity of idols, so He mentioned after it the attributes by which divinity is realized. Know that we have explained in several places of this book that the proofs which God, exalted, mentioned to establish His divinity are either celestial (falakiyyah) or elemental (unsuriyyah). As for the celestial proofs, they are of several kinds:

The first: the creation of the heavens and the earth. This meaning indicates the existence of the Powerful God from many aspects, which we explained in the commentary on His saying, exalted: ﴿Praise belongs to God, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 1].

[p. 213]

The second: the alternation of the states of night and day, and this is what is meant here by His saying: ﴿He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night﴾. This is because light and darkness are two awesome, great armies, and each day one of them overcomes the other at times, and the other overcomes it at other times. This indicates that each of them is overcome and subdued, and there must be a dominant Subduer over both, under whose management and dominion they are, and He is God, glorified and exalted. The meaning of this "wrapping" is that He adds to each of them by the amount that the other loses. As for the meaning of the wrapping of night and day, it is what was narrated in the hadith: "We seek refuge in God from al-hawr after al-kawr," meaning from turning back after advancing. Know that He, glorified and exalted, expressed this meaning by His saying: ﴿He wraps the night over the day﴾, and by His saying: ﴿He covers the night with the day﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], and by His saying: ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day﴾ [al-Hajj: 61], and by His saying: ﴿And it is He who made the night and the day in succession for whoever wishes to remember﴾ [al-Furqan: 62].

The third: considering the states of the stars, especially the sun and the moon, for the sun is the sultan of the day and the moon is the sultan of the night, and most of the interests of this world are bound to them. His saying: ﴿each runs for a specified term﴾: the specified term is the Day of Resurrection. They continue to run until this day, and when the Day of Resurrection comes, they will be gone. Its parallel is His saying, exalted: ﴿and the sun and the moon are joined﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 9]. The meaning of this subjection is that these spheres revolve like the revolving of a waterwheel (manjanun) in one fixed manner until the Day of Resurrection, and at that time the sky will be folded up like the folding of a scroll for documents.

When God mentioned these three types of celestial proofs, He said: ﴿Unquestionably, He is the Mighty, the Ever-Forgiving.﴾ The meaning is that the creation of these great bodies, although it indicates that He is Mighty, that is, of perfect power, He is also Ever-Forgiving, of great mercy, bounty, and beneficence. For when information about His being of great power produces fear and awe, His being Ever-Forgiving produces abundant mercy, and abundant mercy produces hope and desire. Then He, exalted, followed the mention of the celestial proofs with the mention of proofs drawn from this lower world. He began with mentioning the human being, saying: ﴿He created you from a single soul, then made from it its mate﴾. The proof of the human being's coming into existence as indicating the God who chooses has been explained many times before.

If it is said: How is it permissible to say ﴿He created you from a single soul, then made from it its mate﴾ when the mate was created before their creation? They answered this from several aspects:

The first: just as the word "then" (thumma) comes to indicate that one of two events occurred later than the second, so too it comes to indicate that one of two statements is later than the other, like the speaker's saying: "What you did today has reached me, then what you did yesterday was more astonishing," and he also says: "I gave you something today, then what I gave you yesterday was more."

The second: that the sense is "He created you from a soul that was created alone, then its mate was made from it."

The third: God, exalted, brought forth the offspring of Adam from his back like particles (dharr), then after that He created Eve.

Know that when He, exalted, mentioned the argument from His creation of the human being for the existence of the Creator, He mentioned after it the argument from the existence of animals for Him, saying: ﴿and He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾. These are: camels, cattle, sheep, and goats. We have explained how these animals indicate the existence of the Creator in His saying: ﴿and the livestock, He created them for you; in them is warmth﴾ [al-Nahl: 5]. Regarding His saying: ﴿and He sent down for you﴾, there are several aspects:

The first: that God's decree, His determination, and His judgment are described as descending from heaven, because He wrote in the Preserved Tablet every existent that will exist.

The second: that none of the animals lives except by plants, and plants do not subsist except by water and soil, and water descends from heaven. So the sense becomes as if He sent them down.

The third: that He, exalted, created them in Paradise and then sent them down to the earth. His saying: ﴿eight pairs﴾ means a male and a female of the camel, cattle, sheep, and goats. The word "pair" (zawj) is a name for each one that has another with it; when it stands alone, it is a single (fard) of that. He, exalted, said: ﴿and He made from it the two mates, the male and the female﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39].

[p. 214]

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation﴾, and in this there are discussions:

The first: Hamzah read "ummahatikum" with a kasrah on the alif and the mim; al-Kisa'i read it with a kasrah on the hamzah and a fatḥah on the mim; and the rest read "ummahatikum" with a ḍammah on the alif and a fatḥah on the mim.

The second: when He, exalted, mentioned the creation of people from one person, namely Adam, peace be upon him, He followed it with the creation of livestock. He specifically mentioned them because they are the most noble of animals after the human being. Then, after mentioning these two, He mentioned a state shared between the human being and the livestock, namely their being created in the wombs of their mothers. His saying: ﴿creation after creation﴾ means what God mentioned in His saying: ﴿And We created the human being from an extract of clay﴾ ﴿then We made him a drop in a firm lodging﴾ ﴿then We created the drop a clinging clot, then We created the clot a lump, then We created the lump bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced him as another creation. So blessed is God, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12–14]. As for His saying: ﴿in three darknesses﴾, it has been said: the three darknesses are the belly, the womb, and the placenta. It has also been said: the loin, the womb, and the belly. The aspect of argument from these states has been explained in our commentary on His saying: ﴿He is the One who forms you in the wombs however He wills﴾ [Al 'Imran: 6].

Know that when He, exalted, explained these proofs and described them, He said: ﴿That is God, your Lord﴾. That is, that thing whose wondrous acts you have come to know is God, your Lord. In this verse there is an indication that He, glorified and exalted, is free of parts and limbs, and that He is free of corporeality (jismiyyah) and of being in a place (makaniyyah). This is because when He, exalted, wanted to make His servants know His particular essence, He mentioned only His being the doer of these things. Had He been a body composed of limbs, His definition by those parts and limbs would have been a definition of a thing by the parts of its reality. As for defining Him by His states, acts, and effects, that is a definition of Him by matters external to His essence, and the first definition is more complete than the second. Had that first kind been possible, relying on this second kind would have been a shortcoming and a deficiency, and that is impermissible. So we know that relying on this second kind was only good because the first kind is impossible and impossible to exist. This indicates that He, glorified and exalted, is exalted above corporeality, limbs, and parts.

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿To Him belongs the dominion﴾. This indicates restriction: that is, dominion belongs to Him and not to anyone else. Since it is established that there is no dominion except His, it is necessary to say that there is no god but Him, for if another god were established, that god would either have dominion or not have dominion. If he has dominion, then each of them would be an owner and a capable one, and mutual obstruction would take place between them, as established in His saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than God, both would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22], and that is impossible. If the second has no part of power or dominion, then he would be deficient and not fit for divinity. So it is established that when the proof indicates that there is no dominion except for God, it is necessary to say: there is no god for the worlds and no object of worship for all creation except God, the One, the Real, the Eternal Refuge.

Then know that when He, glorified, explained with these proofs the perfection of God's power, wisdom, and mercy, He arranged upon it the refutation of the way of the polytheists and the misguided from several aspects:

The first: His saying: ﴿so how are you turned away?﴾. Our companions (the Ash'arites) argue with it, and the Mu'tazilah also argue with it. As for our companions, the aspect of argument for them from this verse is that it is explicit that they did not turn themselves away from these clear proofs; rather, someone else turned them away from them, and that other is none but God. Also, the proof of reason strengthens this, because every person wants for himself the attainment of truth and correctness. When that is not achieved, and only ignorance and misguidance occur, we know that it comes from another, not from himself. As for the Mu'tazilah, the aspect of argument for them is that His saying ﴿so how are you turned away?﴾ is an expression of wonder at this turning away, and if the agent of that turning were God, exalted, this wonder would have no meaning.

[p. 215]

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed God is free of need of you﴾. The meaning is that God, exalted, did not impose obligations on those who are obligated in order to draw any benefit to Himself or to repel any harm from Himself, because He, exalted, is absolutely self-sufficient, and bringing benefit or repelling harm is impossible with respect to Him. We only said that He is self-sufficient for several reasons:

The first: that He is necessarily existent in His essence, and necessarily existent in all His attributes, and whoever is like this is absolutely self-sufficient.

The second: that if He were in need, that need would either be eternal or temporal. The first is false, for otherwise it would follow that He would create in eternity what He needed, and that is impossible, because creation and eternity are contradictory. The second is also false, because need is a deficiency, and the Wise One is not driven by a motive to acquire a deficiency for Himself.

The third: suppose that doubt remains as to whether craving, aversion, and need can be attributed to Him or not. Is it not known by necessity that the God who is able to create the heavens and the earth, the sun, the moon, the stars, the Throne, the Footstool, the four elements, and the three generated kinds (mawalid) is impossible to benefit from the prayer of Zayd and the fasting of 'Amr, and impossible to be harmed by the non-prayer of this one and the non-fasting of that one? Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that if all the worlds disbelieved and persisted in ignorance, God would still be free of need of them.

Then He, exalted, said after this: ﴿and He does not approve disbelief for His servants﴾. That is to say: although He is not benefited by belief nor harmed by disbelief, He does not approve of disbelief. Al-Jubba'i argued with this verse in two ways:

The first: the Mujbirah (determinists) say that God, exalted, created the disbelief of the servants, and that from the standpoint of what He created it is true and correct. He (al-Jubba'i) said: if the matter were so, then He would have approved disbelief from the aspect in which He created it, and that is the opposite of the verse.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 39, verses 5–7 (part 2 of 2):

The second argument: If disbelief were by the decree of Allah the Exalted, then we would be obligated to be content with it, because contentment with the decree of Allah the Exalted is obligatory. Since the community has agreed that being content with disbelief is disbelief, it is established that it is not by the decree of Allah, and it is also not by the pleasure of Allah the Exalted. Our companions (al-Ashab, the scholars of our theological school) answered this argument in several ways:

The first: The practice of the Qur'an is to restrict the word *'ibad* (servants) to the believers. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ [al-Furqan: 63], and He says: ﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah drink﴾ [al-Insan: 6], and He says: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ [al-Hijr: 42]. Accordingly, on this reading, His statement ﴿and He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾ means that He does not approve disbelief for the believers, and that does not harm us.

The second: We say that disbelief is by the will of Allah the Exalted, but we do not say that it is by the pleasure of Allah. This is because *ridá* (contentment, pleasure) is an expression of praise for an act and approval of it. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Allah was certainly pleased with the believers﴾ [al-Fath: 18], meaning that He praises them and commends them.

The third: Our father, the Shaykh Diya' al-Din Umar, may Allah have mercy on him, used to say: *ridá* is an expression for abandoning blame and objection, and it is not an expression for will. The evidence for this is the verse of Ibn Durayd:

*I was content by compulsion, and contentment under compulsion is the contentment of one who was angry at the turning of fate.*

He affirmed *ridá* together with compulsion (*qasr*), and this indicates what we have said.

The fourth: Grant that *ridá* means will. Still, His statement ﴿and He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾ is general, so restricting it to the verses which indicate that He wills disbelief from the disbeliever is like His statement: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills﴾ [al-Insan: 30]. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if you are grateful, He approves it for you﴾. The meaning is that, when He had explained that He does not approve disbelief, He explained that He approves gratitude. There are several issues here:

The first issue: The reciters differed over the *ha'* in *yarḍahu* (يَرْضَهُ) in three ways:

The first: Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Hamzah read it with a *ḍammah* on the *ha'*, *mukhtalasah* (brief, weakly pronounced) and not followed by a *waw*.

The second: Abu 'Amr and Hamzah, in some transmissions, read *yarḍah* (يَرْضَهْ) with a *sukun* on the *ha'*, for lightness.

The third: Nafi', in some transmissions, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read it with a *ḍammah* on the *ha'* and *mushba'ah* (fully pronounced).

Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Among the reciters are those who fully pronounced the *ha'* until they attached a *waw* to it, because the letter before the *ha'* is vowelled, so it became in the position of *ḍaraba-hu* (ضَرَبَهُ) and *lahu* (لَهُ). Just as this is fully pronounced according to all, so likewise *yarḍahu* (يَرْضَهُ). Among them are those who vowelled the *ha'* and did not add the *waw*, because the original form is *yarḍāhu* (يَرْضاهُ), and the *alif* which is deleted for the *jazm* (apocopation) is not necessarily deleted, so it is like the remaining one. And with the *alif* remaining, it is not permissible to add the *waw*; so likewise here.

The second issue: Gratitude (*shukr*) is a compound state made of speech, belief and action. As for speech, it is the acknowledgment that the blessing has occurred. As for belief, it is the belief that the blessing has come from that benefactor.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾. Al-Jubba'i said: This indicates that Allah the Exalted does not punish anyone for the act of another. So if Allah created their disbelief, it would not be permissible for Him to punish them for it. Also, it is not permissible for children to be punished for the sins of their fathers, unlike what the others say. Those who deny that the blood money (*diyah*) must be imposed on the 'aqilah (paternal kin) also argued from this verse.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then to your Lord is your return﴾. Know that we have mentioned many times that the most important matters for a human being are: to know his Creator to the extent possible; to know what harms him and what benefits him in this worldly life; and to know his state after death. In this verse, He mentioned many proofs from the higher world and the lower world concerning the perfection of the Creator's power, knowledge and wisdom. Then He followed this by commanding gratitude and forbidding disbelief. Then He explained the state of the human after death by His saying: ﴿Then to your Lord is your return﴾. There are issues here:

The first issue: The Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists) held onto the word *ilá* (إلى, "to") as evidence that the God of the universe is in a direction. We have answered this many times.

The second issue: The people (the proponents of the pre-existence of souls) claimed that these souls existed before the bodies, and they held onto the word "return" (*rujū'*) which occurs in this verse and in other verses.

The third issue: This verse indicates the affirmation of resurrection (*ba'th*) and the Last Day (*qiyamah*).

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Then He will inform you of what you used to do﴾. This is a warning to the disobedient and good news to the obedient. His statement, ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾, serves as the reason for what preceded it. That is, He is able to inform you of your deeds, because He is knowing of all that is known. So He knows what is in your hearts of motives and deterrents. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, Allah does not look at your forms or your words, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds."

[Page 216]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 39, verse 8–9:

Page 217
His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance. Then when He grants him a favour from Himself, he forgets what he had been calling upon Him for before, and sets up rivals to God in order to lead [others] astray from His way. Say: "Enjoy your disbelief for a little; indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire."﴾ ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord [equal to the one who does not]? Say: "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?" Only those with understanding are reminded.﴾

Know that when God, may He be exalted, explained the corruption of the view of associating partners with God, and explained that God, may He be exalted, is the One who must be worshipped, He explained in this verse that the way of these disbelievers who worship idols is contradictory. This is because when some kind of harm touches them, they seek its removal only from God; and when that harm departs from them, they return to worshipping idols. It is well known that they turned to God, may He be exalted, only at the occurrence of harm, because He is the One able to bring about good and avert harm. And if they recognise that the matter is so in some circumstances, it is obligatory upon them to acknowledge it in all circumstances. Thus it is established that their way in this matter is contradictory.

As for His saying, ﴿And when harm touches man﴾: it has been said that "man" refers to specific individuals, such as Utbah ibn Rabi'ah and others. It has also been said that it refers to the disbeliever mentioned earlier, because speech is directed toward something previously mentioned.

As for His saying ﴿harm﴾: it includes all adversities, whether in his body, his property, his family or his children, because the word is unrestricted, so there is no sense in restricting it. And ﴿he calls upon his Lord﴾ means he seeks refuge in his Lord and calls out to Him, and hopes for nothing else to remove the harm. Therefore He said ﴿turning to Him in repentance﴾, meaning returning to Him alone in removing that harm, because inábah is returning. ﴿Then when He grants him a favour from Himself﴾, meaning He gives him. The author of al-Kashshaf said: regarding its real meaning there are two possibilities:

The first: He made him a manager of wealth, from their saying: "he is a khā'il of wealth" and "khāl of wealth", when he takes care of it and manages it well. From this is what is reported from the Messenger of God ﴿ﷺ﴾: "that he would take care of his companions (yatakhawwalu) with admonition."

The second: He made him one who swaggers (yakhūlu), from khāla yakhūlu, when one behaves arrogantly and boasts. In this sense the Arabs said:

Indeed the wealthy man has a long train, and is swaggering.

* * *
Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿he forgets what he had been calling upon Him for before﴾, meaning he forgets his Lord whom he had been humbly beseeching and imploring. The word "mā" here means "man", as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and He who created the male and the female﴾ [al-Layl: 3], His saying: ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ [al-Kafirun: 3], and His saying: ﴿so marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [an-Nisa: 3]. It has also been said: he forgot the harm for which he had been calling upon God to remove it. The meaning of "forgets" is that he abandoned his supplication, as if he had not turned to his Lord. Had He meant genuine forgetting, He would not have blamed him for it. It is also possible that the meaning is that he forgot that he should not be afraid, and that there is no god besides Him, so he returned to taking partners with God.
* * *
Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and sets up rivals to God in order to lead [others] astray from His way﴾, and in this there are issues:

The first issue: Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿liyaḍilla﴾ with a fatḥah on the yā', while the others read ﴿liyuḍilla﴾ with a ḍammah on the yā', in the sense of leading others astray.

The second issue: The meaning is that He, may He be exalted, astonishes rational people at the contradiction of these two states: in the time of harm they believe there is no refuge but Him, and in the time of blessing they return to taking gods along with Him. It is well known that if He is sought only in the time of harm because He is the One able to bring about good and evil, then this meaning remains in the time of ease and leisure as well. So describing their condition in these two times involves contradiction and lack of intellect.

Page 218
The third issue: The meaning of His saying ﴿to lead [others] astray from His way﴾ is that he does not limit himself to leading himself astray, but calls others, either by his deed or his words, to share in that, so that he increases in sin upon his sin. The lām in ﴿liyuḍilla﴾ is the lām of consequence, as in His saying: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. When God mentioned this contradictory act of theirs, He threatened them, saying: ﴿Say: "Enjoy your disbelief for a little"﴾. What is meant is not a command but a rebuke, and to inform him of the brevity of his enjoyment in this world, and then his destination will be the Fire.

When God explained the attributes of the polytheists and the misguided, and then their clinging to other than God, He followed it with an explanation of the circumstances of the people of truth, who have no return except to God and no reliance except on God's bounty. So He said: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing﴾. In this there are issues:

The first issue: Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Hamzah read ﴿amman﴾ with a light mīm, while the rest read it with a shaddah. As for the light reading, there are two possibilities:

The first: the alif is the interrogative alif entering upon "man", and the answer is omitted, with the implied meaning: "is one who is not like that [equal to the one who is]?" It has also been said: "like the one who set up rivals to God", relying on what has been mentioned before.

The second: that it is the alif of address, as if it were said: "O one who is devoutly obedient, from the people of Paradise". As for the shaddah, al-Farra' said: the original is "am man", and the mīm was assimilated into the mīm, and on this view it is the am of your saying: "Is Zayd better, or 'Amr?"

The second issue: al-qānit is one who stands fulfilling what is obligatory upon him of obedience. From this is his saying: "The best prayer is the prayer of qunut", which means standing in it; and from it is the qunut in the Subh prayer, because one supplicates standing. It is reported from Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "I do not know qunut except as reciting the Qur'an and prolonging the standing", and he recited: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient﴾. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: qunut is obedience to God, due to His saying: ﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 116], meaning obedient. It is reported from Qatadah: "ātā' al-layl" means the hours of the night, its beginning, middle and end. In this word there is an indication of the excellence of night prayer, and that it is superior to standing in the day. Several points confirm this:

First: worship at night is more hidden from eyes, so it is further from showing off.

Second: darkness prevents seeing, and the sleep of creatures prevents hearing; so when the heart becomes free from preoccupation with external circumstances, it returns to the original goal, which is knowing God and serving Him.

Third: night is the time of sleep, so abandoning it is harder, and therefore the reward is greater.

Fourth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the rising of the night is more firm in tread and more upright in speech﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 6]. His saying ﴿prostrating﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). It has been read ﴿sājidun wa qā'imun﴾, as a predicate following a predicate, and the waw is for combining the two attributes.

Know that this verse indicates wondrous secrets:

The first of these is that it begins with mention of knowledge and ends with mention of knowledge. As for action, it is his being devoutly obedient, prostrating and standing; as for knowledge, it is His saying: ﴿Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾ This indicates that human perfection is confined to these two aims: action is the beginning, and knowledge and unveiling is the end.

The second benefit: He, may He be exalted, drew attention to the fact that benefit from action is only obtained when a person is constant in it, for qunut is an expression for a man standing in what is obligatory upon him of acts of obedience. This indicates that knowledge is only beneficial when a person is persistent in it. His saying ﴿prostrating and standing﴾ refers to the kinds of actions. His saying ﴿fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord﴾ refers to the fact that when a person is persistent, there is first unveiled to him the station of majesty, which is His saying ﴿fearing the Hereafter﴾, then after it the station of mercy, which is His saying ﴿hoping for the mercy of his Lord﴾; then various kinds of unveilings occur, and this is what is meant by His saying ﴿Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾

Page 219
The third benefit: in the station of fear He said ﴿fearing the Hereafter﴾, without attributing the fear to Himself, and in the station of hope He attributed it to Himself. This indicates that the side of hope is more perfect and more fitting in the presence of God, may He be exalted.

The third issue: It has been said that what is meant by His saying ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night﴾ is ʿUthman, because he used to revive the night in a single rak'ah and recite the Qur'an in a single rak'ah. The correct view is that what is meant is everyone who is described by this attribute, so ʿUthman and others are included, because the verse is not restricted to him.

The fourth issue: There is no doubt that there is an elision in the speech, and the implied meaning is: "Is one who is devoutly obedient like others?" This elision is fine because the context indicates it: before this verse He mentioned the disbeliever, and after it He said: ﴿Say: "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?"﴾ The implied sense of the verse is: "Say: 'Are those who know equal to those who do not know?'" Those who know are those whose attribute is that they are devoutly obedient in the hours of the night, prostrating and standing; and those who do not know are those whose description, at times of trial and fear, is that they affirm God's oneness, and at times of ease and leisure, that they associate partners. When we posit this implied sense, the meaning becomes clear. God described the disbelievers as not knowing because, although God gave them the instruments of knowledge, they turned away from acquiring knowledge; for this reason He made them as if they were not people of understanding, since they did not benefit from their intellects and hearts.

* * *
As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?"﴾, it is a great reminder of the excellence of knowledge. We have elaborated this meaning in our commentary on His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31]. The author of al-Kashshaf said: by "those who know" he means those previously mentioned, who are the devoutly obedient, and by "those who do not know" he means those who do not perform this act; as if he made the devoutly obedient the scholars. This is a reminder that whoever acts is not ignorant. He then said: there is in it a great disparagement of those who master the sciences but do not practise devotion, who issue legal opinions and then are tested by worldly things; they are, in God's sight, ignorant.
* * *
Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Only those with understanding are reminded﴾. He means that this great disparity between the scholars and the ignorant is also not recognised except by people of understanding. It was said to one of the scholars: "You say that knowledge is better than wealth, yet we see scholars gathering at the doors of kings, and we do not see kings gathering at the doors of scholars." The scholar replied that this also indicates the excellence of knowledge, because scholars know the benefits in wealth and so seek it, while the ignorant did not know the benefits in knowledge, so inevitably they abandoned it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 39, verse 10–16 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: O My servants who have believed, fear your Lord. For those who do good in this world there is good, and the earth of Allah is spacious. Indeed, those who are patient will be given their reward without account.﴾ ﴿Say: Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion.﴾ ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims.﴾ ﴿Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great day.﴾ ﴿Say: It is Allah I worship, being sincere to Him in my religion. Know that when He, may He be exalted, explained the negation of equality between those who know and those who do not know, He followed it by commanding His Messenger to address the believers with various kinds of speech:

The first kind: His saying: ﴿Say: O My servants who have believed, fear your Lord.﴾ The meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, commanded the believers to add taqwa (God-consciousness) to faith. This is among the first proofs that faith remains alongside disobedience. The judge (al-Qadi) said: He commanded them to taqwa so that they would not nullify their faith, because when they guard against major sins their reward remains safe for them, and by committing them it is nullified. It is said to him: this indicates the opposite of your claim is more appropriate, because when He commanded the believers to taqwa, that indicates that they remain believers in the absence of taqwa, and that indicates that immorality does not remove faith.

Know that when He, exalted is He, commanded the believers to guard themselves, He explained to them the benefits of this guarding, so He said: ﴿For those who do good in this world there is good.﴾ His saying ﴿in this world﴾ may be connected either to His saying ﴿do good﴾ or to "good." On the first reading, its meaning is: for those who do good in this world, all of them, there is good in the Hereafter, which is entry into Paradise. The indefiniteness in His saying ﴿good﴾ is for magnification, meaning: a good beyond which the intellect cannot reach the full reality of its perfection.

As for the second reading, its meaning is: those who do good, for them in this world there is good. Those who hold this view said: this good is health and well-being. I say: it is better to interpret it as the three mentioned in his saying ﴿ﷺ﴾: "Three things have no limit: security, health, and sufficiency." Some people said: the first view is more appropriate, and this is supported by several considerations:

The first: the indefiniteness in His saying ﴿good﴾ indicates supremacy, exaltedness and loftiness, which does not befit the conditions of this world, for it is lowly and transient, but befits the conditions of the Hereafter, for it is noble and safe from ending and perishing.

The second: the reward of the one who does good through monotheism and righteous deeds is only obtained in the Hereafter. He, exalted, said: ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned﴾ [Ghafir: 17]. Also, the worldly blessings of health, security and sufficiency are obtained by the disbelievers too. Moreover, their attainment by the disbeliever is greater and more complete than their attainment by the believer, as he ﷺ said: "This world is a prison for the believer and a paradise for the disbeliever." And He, exalted, said: ﴿Had We not feared that people would become one community, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver roofs for their houses and stairways by which they ascend﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 33].

The third: His saying ﴿For those who do good in this world there is good﴾ conveys restriction, meaning that the good of this world is attained only by those who do good. This is false. But if we take this good as the good of the Hereafter, this restriction is valid. Thus interpreting it as the good of the Hereafter is more appropriate. Then Allah, exalted, said: ﴿And the earth of Allah is spacious,﴾ and concerning it there are two views:

The first: the meaning is that there is absolutely no excuse for those who fall short in doing good, even if they plead their homelands and countries, and that they cannot devote themselves to doing good and directing their resolve toward it there. Say to them: indeed the earth of Allah is spacious and His lands are many, so migrate from these lands to lands where you can be occupied with acts of obedience and worship, and follow the examples of the prophets and righteous ones

in their migration to other than their lands, so that they may increase in good upon their good and in obedience upon their obedience. They said, "We were oppressed in the land." They said, "Was not the earth of Allah spacious, so that you could emigrate therein?"﴾ [An-Nisa: 97].

The second view: Abu Muslim said: it is not impossible that the intended meaning of "the earth" is the earth of Paradise. This is because He, exalted, commanded the believers to taqwa, which is fear of Allah, then explained that whoever is God-conscious, for him in the Hereafter is good, which is eternal abiding in Paradise. Then He explained that the earth of Allah, that is His Paradise, is spacious, due to His saying: ﴿We shall settle in Paradise wherever we will﴾ [Az-Zumar: 74], and His saying: ﴿A Paradise whose width is the heavens and the earth, prepared for the righteous﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133]. But the first view is preferable to me, because His saying ﴿Indeed, those who are patient will be given their reward without account﴾ befits only the first.

In this verse there are issues:

* * *

First issue: As for the detailed discussion of the reality of patience, we have mentioned it in Surat al-Baqarah. The intended meaning here by "the patient" is those who were patient in leaving their homelands and kin, in swallowing bitter draughts, and in bearing trials in obedience to Allah, exalted is He.

Second issue: Calling the benefits that Allah promised for patience a "reward" may give the impression that the deed earns the reward, since reward is what is deserved. However, decisive proofs establish that the deed does not make reward obligatory, so the word "reward" must be taken as a reward according to the promise, not according to entitlement.

Third issue: He, exalted, described that reward as "without account," and concerning this there are several views:

The first: al-Jubba'i said: the meaning is that they are given what they deserve and more by way of bounty, so it is "without account." Had they been given only what they deserved, that would have been an account. The judge (al-Qadi) said: this is not correct, because Allah, exalted, described the reward as "without account," and even if they were given only the reward they deserve, the reward is other than bounty.

The second: the reward has three attributes:
One: that it is a perpetual reward for them. His saying ﴿without account﴾ means without end, because everything that falls under account is finite, so what has no end is outside account.
Second: that its benefits are complete in themselves, and the intellect of the obedient one could never reach the full reality of that reward. He ﷺ said: "In Paradise there is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." Every kind of reward they witness they find greater than what they imagined and expected, and what a person does not expect may be said to be not within his reckoning. So His saying ﴿without account﴾ is taken in this sense. The third interpretation is that the reward of the people of trial cannot be measured by balance or measure. Ṣāḥib al-Kashshaf narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "On the Day of Resurrection Allah will set up the scales. The people of prayer will come and their rewards will be weighed out for them by the scales, and the people of charity will come and their rewards will be weighed out for them by the scales, and the people of trial will come, and no scale will be set up for them nor any register unfolded for them, and reward will be poured out upon them in a torrent." Allah, exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who are patient will be given their reward without account,﴾ so that the people of well-being in this world wish that their bodies were cut with shears because of the excellence the people of trial have.

The second kind of the explanations which Allah commanded His Messenger to mention is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion.﴾ Muqatil said: The disbelievers of Quraysh said to the Prophet ﷺ: "What drives you to this religion which you have brought us? Do you not look at the religion of your father and grandfather and the leaders of your people, who worship al-Lat and al-'Uzza?" So Allah revealed: "Say, O Muhammad, indeed I have been commanded to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion."

I say: Obligation is of two kinds:
One of them: the command to refrain from what is not fitting.
The second: the command to attain what is fitting. The first level takes precedence over the second according to the necessary, binding rank. Having established this, we say: He, exalted, placed first the command to remove what is not fitting, saying ﴿fear your Lord﴾, because taqwa is refraining from what is not fitting. Then immediately after it He mentioned the command to attain what is fitting, saying ﴿Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion.﴾ This comprises two conditions:
One: the command to worship Allah.
Second: that this worship be free from the taints of overt shirk and the taints of hidden shirk. Allah, exalted, specified the Messenger with this command in order to alert that others are more entitled to it; so it is like an encouragement to others. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims﴾ undoubtedly means: I am the first to adhere to the acts of worship with which I was sent. In this verse there are two benefits:

The first benefit: it is as if he says: I am not one of the tyrannical kings who command people to things they themselves do not do; rather, everything I have commanded you to do, I am the first of people to begin it and the most constant in it.

The second benefit: He said ﴿I have been commanded to worship Allah﴾, and worship has two pillars: the work of the heart and the work of the limbs. The work of the heart is more noble than the work of the limbs, so He mentioned first the nobler part, which is His saying ﴿being sincere to Him in religion﴾, then immediately after it mentioned the lesser, which is the work of the limbs, namely Islam, for the Prophet ﷺ explained Islam in the report about Jibril, peace be upon him, as the outward deeds, and this is what is meant by His saying in this verse: ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims.﴾ Nor may anyone say: what is the benefit of repeating the word "commanded"? We answer: the word "commanded" is mentioned first with the work of the heart and second with the work of the limbs, so this is not repetition.

The third benefit in His saying ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims﴾ is an alert that being a Messenger from Allah is obligatory to obey, because the first of the Muslims in the laws of Allah can only be the Messenger of Allah, since the first to know those laws and obligations is the Messenger who conveys them. When Allah, exalted, clarified his command to sincerity in the heart and to the specific deeds, and the command may admit of obligation or recommendation, He clarified that this command is for obligation, so He said: ﴿Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great day.﴾ In this there are benefits:

The first benefit: Allah commanded Muhammad ﷺ to apply this statement to himself, and the purpose is to intensify the warning to others against sins, for if, despite his great rank and the nobility of his prophethood, he must be fearful and wary of sins, then others are more deserving of that.

The second benefit: the verse indicates that what is entailed by disobedience is not the occurrence of punishment but fear of punishment. This accords with our statement that Allah, exalted, may pardon the sinner and the major sin, so the necessary consequence upon the occurrence of disobedience is fear of punishment, not the actual occurrence of punishment.

The third benefit: this verse indicates that the apparent meaning of a command is obligation, because He said at the beginning of the verse: ﴿Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah,﴾ then after it said: ﴿Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great day.﴾ So the meaning of this disobedience is abandoning the command mentioned earlier, and this requires that one who abandons the command is disobedient, and the disobedient is subject to fear of punishment, and there is no meaning of obligation except that.

Page 223

**The third type of thing that Allah commanded His Messenger to mention is His saying:** ﴿Say: It is Allah I worship, sincere in my religion to Him.﴾ If it is asked: what is the meaning of the repetition in His saying ﴿Say: I have been commanded to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ and His saying ﴿Say: It is Allah I worship, sincere in my religion to Him﴾? We say: this is not a repetition, because the first is an informing that he is commanded by Allah to perform worship, and the second is an informing that he was commanded not to worship anyone other than Him. This is because His saying ﴿I have been commanded to worship Allah﴾ does not imply exclusivity (*hasr*), whereas His exalted saying ﴿It is Allah I worship﴾ does imply exclusivity, meaning: I worship Allah and do not worship anyone besides Him. The evidence for this is that after He said ﴿It is Allah I worship﴾, He said after it: ﴿Worship what you will besides Him﴾. There is no doubt that His saying ﴿Worship what you will besides Him﴾ is not a command, but rather its purpose is a rebuke (*zajr*), as if He is saying: since the clarification regarding the obligation of upholding monotheism has reached its utmost limit, then after this you are more knowledgeable about yourselves. Then He explained the completeness of the rebuke with His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed the losers are those who have lost themselves﴾, because of their falling into a destruction beyond which no destruction can be conceived, ﴿and their families [as well]﴾, because if they are among the people of the Fire, they have lost them just as they lost themselves, and if they are among the people of Paradise, they have departed from them with a departure after which there is absolutely no return. Ibn ʿAbbas said: indeed every man has a dwelling, a family and servants in Paradise; if he obeys, he is given that, and if he is among the people of the Fire, he is deprived of that, so he has lost his self, his family and his dwelling, and others among the Muslims inherit it. The *khasir* (loser) is the one who is defrauded. When Allah explained their loss, He described that loss with the utmost horribleness, saying: ﴿Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss﴾, so the repetition was for the sake of emphasis.

**The second:** He, exalted, mentioned at the beginning of this statement the particle ﴿*alā*﴾ (unquestionably), which is for alerting, and mentioning alerting in this place indicates magnification, as if it were said: He has reached such greatness that your minds cannot attain to it, so be alert to it.

**The third:** the word ﴿*huwa*﴾ (it) in His saying ﴿It is the manifest loss﴾ implies exclusivity, as if it were said: every loss, when set against it, is as if it were no loss at all.

**The fourth:** describing it as ﴿manifest﴾ indicates awe-inspiring severity. I say: We have already explained that the wording of the verse indicates that it is a manifest loss, so let us now clarify, according to rational investigations, that it is a manifest loss. I say: we need to explain two matters: that it is a loss, and then that it is manifest. As for the first, its explanation is that He, exalted, gave this life, gave the intellect, and gave capacity, and all of that is the capital. As for this life, its purpose is that one may acquire within it a good life in the Hereafter.

* * *

As for the intellect, it is an expression for the self-evident knowledge, and this self-evident knowledge is the capital. Reflection and thinking have no meaning except arranging knowledge so that through that arrangement one may reach the acquisition of acquired knowledge. Thus, that self-evident knowledge called the intellect is the capital, and its composition in specific ways resembles the merchant's handling of his capital, and its composition in ways of buying and selling. The attainment of knowledge of the conclusion resembles the attainment of profit. Likewise, the attainment of the capacity for deeds resembles the capital, and the use of that power in attaining deeds of righteousness and goodness resembles the merchant's handling of his capital, and the attainment of deeds of righteousness and goodness resembles profit. Once this is established, we say: whoever Allah has given life, intellect and capacity, and then he has not benefited from them either the knowledge of the truth or the performance of good at all, he has been deprived of profit entirely, and when he dies the capital is wholly lost, and that is a loss. This is the explanation of its being a loss.

As for the second, which is the explanation that this loss is manifest: whoever does not gain an increase, but nonetheless is safe from calamities and harms, then just as he has not obtained an additional benefit, he has also not obtained an additional harm. As for these disbelievers, they have used their intellects, which are their capital, in extracting the aspects of doubts and strengthening ignorance and misguidance, and they have used their powers and capacities in deeds of evil, falsehood and corruption. Thus they have combined matters that are in the utmost baseness:

First: they have exhausted their bodies and their intellects in seeking those false beliefs and corrupt deeds.

[p. 224]

Second: when they die, the capital is lost from them without any benefit.

Third: those severe hardships that existed in the world in support of those misguidances become causes for severe punishment and great affliction after death. Upon reflecting on these meanings, it becomes clear that no loss can be conceived that is greater than their loss, nor any deprivation greater than their deprivation, and we seek refuge in Allah from it.

When Allah, exalted, explained the states of their deprivation from profit and clarified the manner of their loss, He made clear that they did not limit themselves to deprivation and loss, but added to it the deserving of a great punishment and a severe retribution, so He said: ﴿For them there will be layers of fire above them and layers below﴾. What is meant is the encompassing of the Fire around them from all sides, and its parallel in the inner states is the encompassing of ignorance, deprivation, greed and all the blameworthy traits around a person. If it is asked: the *ẓulal* (layers) are what is above a person, so how is what is beneath him called *ẓulal*? The answer has several aspects:

The first: it is from the category of applying the name of one of two opposites to the other, like His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40].

The second: that which is beneath a person becomes a layer (*ẓulla*) for another person beneath him, because the Fire has degrees (*darakāt*) just as Paradise has ranks (*darajāt*).

The third: when the lower layer resembles the upper layer in heat, burning and harm, the name of one of them is applied to the other because of similarity and resemblance.

Al-Hasan said: they are between two layers of the Fire, not knowing what is above them more than what is beneath them. A parallel to this verse is His exalted saying: ﴿On the Day the punishment will cover them from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 55], and His exalted saying: ﴿For them from Hell is a bed, and above them are coverings﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 41].

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿This is what Allah threatens His servants with﴾, that is, that which has been mentioned previously of the description of the punishment. So His saying ﴿This﴾ is the subject, and His saying ﴿Allah threatens His servants with it﴾ is the predicate. Regarding His saying ﴿Allah threatens His servants with it﴾ there are two opinions:

The first: the meaning is: that punishment prepared for the disbelievers is what Allah threatens His servants with, i.e., the believers, because we have explained that the word *ʿibād* (servants) in the Qur'an is specific to the people of faith. It was a threat to the believers because when they hear that the state of the disbelievers is as has been mentioned, they fear, and so they become sincere in monotheism and obedience.

The second aspect: this statement is in the form of an answer to a question, because it may be said: He, exalted, is independent of the worlds, free of desire, vengeance and the motive to harm, so how is it fitting for Him to punish these wretched people to this great extent? The answer to this is that the purpose of it is to frighten the disbelievers and the misguided away from disbelief and misguidance. When obligation (*taklīf*) is not completed except by frightening, and the frightening is not fully beneficial except by bringing that thing into existence, it becomes necessary to bring that kind of punishment into existence, in order to achieve that aim which is the obligation. However, the first aspect is closer to me, and the evidence for it is that He said after it: ﴿O My servants, so fear Me﴾, and His saying ﴿O My servants﴾ most clearly indicates that what is meant is the believers. The first: the meaning is that there is absolutely no excuse for those who fall short in doing good, even if they plead their homelands and countries, and that they cannot devote themselves to doing good and directing their resolve toward it there. in their migration to other than their lands, so that they may increase in good upon their good and in obedience upon their obedience. They said, "We were oppressed in the land." They said, "Was not the earth of Allah spacious, so that you could emigrate therein?"﴾ [An-Nisa: 97].

The second view: Abu Muslim said: it is not impossible that the intended meaning of "the earth" is the earth of Paradise. This is because He, exalted, commanded the believers to taqwa, which is fear of Allah, then explained that whoever is God-conscious, for him in the Hereafter is good, which is eternal abiding in Paradise. Then He explained that the earth of Allah, that is His Paradise, is spacious, due to His saying: ﴿We shall settle in Paradise wherever we will﴾ [Az-Zumar: 74], and His saying: ﴿A Paradise whose width is the heavens and the earth, prepared for the righteous﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133]. But the first view is preferable to me, because His saying ﴿Indeed, those who are patient will be given their reward without account﴾ befits only the first.

In this verse there are issues:

* * *

First issue: As for the detailed discussion of the reality of patience, we have mentioned it in Surat al-Baqarah. The intended meaning here by "the patient" is those who were patient in leaving their homelands and kin, in swallowing bitter draughts, and in bearing trials in obedience to Allah, exalted is He.

Second issue: Calling the benefits that Allah promised for patience a "reward" may give the impression that the deed earns the reward, since reward is what is deserved. However, decisive proofs establish that the deed does not make reward obligatory, so the word "reward" must be taken as a reward according to the promise, not according to entitlement.

Third issue: He, exalted, described that reward as "without account," and concerning this there are several views:

The first: al-Jubba'i said: the meaning is that they are given what they deserve and more by way of bounty, so it is "without account." Had they been given only what they deserved, that would have been an account. The judge (al-Qadi) said: this is not correct, because Allah, exalted, described the reward as "without account," and even if they were given only the reward they deserve, the reward is other than bounty.

The second: the reward has three attributes:
One: that it is a perpetual reward for them. His saying ﴿without account﴾ means without end, because everything that falls under account is finite, so what has no end is outside account.
Second: that its benefits are complete in themselves, and the intellect of the obedient one could never reach the full reality of that reward. He ﷺ said: "In Paradise there is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." Every kind of reward they witness they find greater than what they imagined and expected, and what a person does not expect may be said to be not within his reckoning. So His saying ﴿without account﴾ is taken in this sense. The third interpretation is that the reward of the people of trial cannot be measured by balance or measure. Ṣāḥib al-Kashshaf narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "On the Day of Resurrection Allah will set up the scales. The people of prayer will come and their rewards will be weighed out for them by the scales, and the people of charity will come and their rewards will be weighed out for them by the scales, and the people of trial will come, and no scale will be set up for them nor any register unfolded for them, and reward will be poured out upon them in a torrent." Allah, exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who are patient will be given their reward without account,﴾ so that the people of well-being in this world wish that their bodies were cut with shears because of the excellence the people of trial have.

The second kind of the explanations which Allah commanded His Messenger to mention is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion.﴾ Muqatil said: The disbelievers of Quraysh said to the Prophet ﷺ: "What drives you to this religion which you have brought us? Do you not look at the religion of your father and grandfather and the leaders of your people, who worship al-Lat and al-'Uzza?" So Allah revealed: "Say, O Muhammad, indeed I have been commanded to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion."

I say: Obligation is of two kinds:
One of them: the command to refrain from what is not fitting.
The second: the command to attain what is fitting. The first level takes precedence over the second according to the necessary, binding rank. Having established this, we say: He, exalted, placed first the command to remove what is not fitting, saying ﴿fear your Lord﴾, because taqwa is refraining from what is not fitting. Then immediately after it He mentioned the command to attain what is fitting, saying ﴿Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion.﴾ This comprises two conditions:
One: the command to worship Allah.
Second: that this worship be free from the taints of overt shirk and the taints of hidden shirk. Allah, exalted, specified the Messenger with this command in order to alert that others are more entitled to it; so it is like an encouragement to others. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims﴾ undoubtedly means: I am the first to adhere to the acts of worship with which I was sent. In this verse there are two benefits:

The first benefit: it is as if he says: I am not one of the tyrannical kings who command people to things they themselves do not do; rather, everything I have commanded you to do, I am the first of people to begin it and the most constant in it.

The second benefit: He said ﴿I have been commanded to worship Allah﴾, and worship has two pillars: the work of the heart and the work of the limbs. The work of the heart is more noble than the work of the limbs, so He mentioned first the nobler part, which is His saying ﴿being sincere to Him in religion﴾, then immediately after it mentioned the lesser, which is the work of the limbs, namely Islam, for the Prophet ﷺ explained Islam in the report about Jibril, peace be upon him, as the outward deeds, and this is what is meant by His saying in this verse: ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims.﴾ Nor may anyone say: what is the benefit of repeating the word "commanded"? We answer: the word "commanded" is mentioned first with the work of the heart and second with the work of the limbs, so this is not repetition.

The third benefit in His saying ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims﴾ is an alert that being a Messenger from Allah is obligatory to obey, because the first of the Muslims in the laws of Allah can only be the Messenger of Allah, since the first to know those laws and obligations is the Messenger who conveys them. When Allah, exalted, clarified his command to sincerity in the heart and to the specific deeds, and the command may admit of obligation or recommendation, He clarified that this command is for obligation, so He said: ﴿Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great day.﴾ In this there are benefits:

The first benefit: Allah commanded Muhammad ﷺ to apply this statement to himself, and the purpose is to intensify the warning to others against sins, for if, despite his great rank and the nobility of his prophethood, he must be fearful and wary of sins, then others are more deserving of that.

The second benefit: the verse indicates that what is entailed by disobedience is not the occurrence of punishment but fear of punishment. This accords with our statement that Allah, exalted, may pardon the sinner and the major sin, so the necessary consequence upon the occurrence of disobedience is fear of punishment, not the actual occurrence of punishment.

The third benefit: this verse indicates that the apparent meaning of a command is obligation, because He said at the beginning of the verse: ﴿Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah,﴾ then after it said: ﴿Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great day.﴾ So the meaning of this disobedience is abandoning the command mentioned earlier, and this requires that one who abandons the command is disobedient, and the disobedient is subject to fear of punishment, and there is no meaning of obligation except that.

**The third type of thing that Allah commanded His Messenger to mention is His saying:** ﴿Say: It is Allah I worship, sincere in my religion to Him.﴾ If it is asked: what is the meaning of the repetition in His saying ﴿Say: I have been commanded to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ and His saying ﴿Say: It is Allah I worship, sincere in my religion to Him﴾? We say: this is not a repetition, because the first is an informing that he is commanded by Allah to perform worship, and the second is an informing that he was commanded not to worship anyone other than Him. This is because His saying ﴿I have been commanded to worship Allah﴾ does not imply exclusivity (*hasr*), whereas His exalted saying ﴿It is Allah I worship﴾ does imply exclusivity, meaning: I worship Allah and do not worship anyone besides Him. The evidence for this is that after He said ﴿It is Allah I worship﴾, He said after it: ﴿Worship what you will besides Him﴾. There is no doubt that His saying ﴿Worship what you will besides Him﴾ is not a command, but rather its purpose is a rebuke (*zajr*), as if He is saying: since the clarification regarding the obligation of upholding monotheism has reached its utmost limit, then after this you are more knowledgeable about yourselves. Then He explained the completeness of the rebuke with His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed the losers are those who have lost themselves﴾, because of their falling into a destruction beyond which no destruction can be conceived, ﴿and their families [as well]﴾, because if they are among the people of the Fire, they have lost them just as they lost themselves, and if they are among the people of Paradise, they have departed from them with a departure after which there is absolutely no return. Ibn ʿAbbas said: indeed every man has a dwelling, a family and servants in Paradise; if he obeys, he is given that, and if he is among the people of the Fire, he is deprived of that, so he has lost his self, his family and his dwelling, and others among the Muslims inherit it. The *khasir* (loser) is the one who is defrauded. When Allah explained their loss, He described that loss with the utmost horribleness, saying: ﴿Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss﴾, so the repetition was for the sake of emphasis.

**The second:** He, exalted, mentioned at the beginning of this statement the particle ﴿*alā*﴾ (unquestionably), which is for alerting, and mentioning alerting in this place indicates magnification, as if it were said: He has reached such greatness that your minds cannot attain to it, so be alert to it.

**The third:** the word ﴿*huwa*﴾ (it) in His saying ﴿It is the manifest loss﴾ implies exclusivity, as if it were said: every loss, when set against it, is as if it were no loss at all.

**The fourth:** describing it as ﴿manifest﴾ indicates awe-inspiring severity. I say: We have already explained that the wording of the verse indicates that it is a manifest loss, so let us now clarify, according to rational investigations, that it is a manifest loss. I say: we need to explain two matters: that it is a loss, and then that it is manifest. As for the first, its explanation is that He, exalted, gave this life, gave the intellect, and gave capacity, and all of that is the capital. As for this life, its purpose is that one may acquire within it a good life in the Hereafter.

* * *

As for the intellect, it is an expression for the self-evident knowledge, and this self-evident knowledge is the capital. Reflection and thinking have no meaning except arranging knowledge so that through that arrangement one may reach the acquisition of acquired knowledge. Thus, that self-evident knowledge called the intellect is the capital, and its composition in specific ways resembles the merchant's handling of his capital, and its composition in ways of buying and selling. The attainment of knowledge of the conclusion resembles the attainment of profit. Likewise, the attainment of the capacity for deeds resembles the capital, and the use of that power in attaining deeds of righteousness and goodness resembles the merchant's handling of his capital, and the attainment of deeds of righteousness and goodness resembles profit. Once this is established, we say: whoever Allah has given life, intellect and capacity, and then he has not benefited from them either the knowledge of the truth or the performance of good at all, he has been deprived of profit entirely, and when he dies the capital is wholly lost, and that is a loss. This is the explanation of its being a loss.

As for the second, which is the explanation that this loss is manifest: whoever does not gain an increase, but nonetheless is safe from calamities and harms, then just as he has not obtained an additional benefit, he has also not obtained an additional harm. As for these disbelievers, they have used their intellects, which are their capital, in extracting the aspects of doubts and strengthening ignorance and misguidance, and they have used their powers and capacities in deeds of evil, falsehood and corruption. Thus they have combined matters that are in the utmost baseness:

First: they have exhausted their bodies and their intellects in seeking those false beliefs and corrupt deeds.

[p. 224]

Second: when they die, the capital is lost from them without any benefit.

Third: those severe hardships that existed in the world in support of those misguidances become causes for severe punishment and great affliction after death. Upon reflecting on these meanings, it becomes clear that no loss can be conceived that is greater than their loss, nor any deprivation greater than their deprivation, and we seek refuge in Allah from it.

When Allah, exalted, explained the states of their deprivation from profit and clarified the manner of their loss, He made clear that they did not limit themselves to deprivation and loss, but added to it the deserving of a great punishment and a severe retribution, so He said: ﴿For them there will be layers of fire above them and layers below﴾. What is meant is the encompassing of the Fire around them from all sides, and its parallel in the inner states is the encompassing of ignorance, deprivation, greed and all the blameworthy traits around a person. If it is asked: the *ẓulal* (layers) are what is above a person, so how is what is beneath him called *ẓulal*? The answer has several aspects:

The first: it is from the category of applying the name of one of two opposites to the other, like His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40].

The second: that which is beneath a person becomes a layer (*ẓulla*) for another person beneath him, because the Fire has degrees (*darakāt*) just as Paradise has ranks (*darajāt*).

The third: when the lower layer resembles the upper layer in heat, burning and harm, the name of one of them is applied to the other because of similarity and resemblance.

Al-Hasan said: they are between two layers of the Fire, not knowing what is above them more than what is beneath them. A parallel to this verse is His exalted saying: ﴿On the Day the punishment will cover them from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 55], and His exalted saying: ﴿For them from Hell is a bed, and above them are coverings﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 41].

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿This is what Allah threatens His servants with﴾, that is, that which has been mentioned previously of the description of the punishment. So His saying ﴿This﴾ is the subject, and His saying ﴿Allah threatens His servants with it﴾ is the predicate. Regarding His saying ﴿Allah threatens His servants with it﴾ there are two opinions:

The first: the meaning is: that punishment prepared for the disbelievers is what Allah threatens His servants with, i.e., the believers, because we have explained that the word *ʿibād* (servants) in the Qur'an is specific to the people of faith. It was a threat to the believers because when they hear that the state of the disbelievers is as has been mentioned, they fear, and so they become sincere in monotheism and obedience.

The second aspect: this statement is in the form of an answer to a question, because it may be said: He, exalted, is independent of the worlds, free of desire, vengeance and the motive to harm, so how is it fitting for Him to punish these wretched people to this great extent? The answer to this is that the purpose of it is to frighten the disbelievers and the misguided away from disbelief and misguidance. When obligation (*taklīf*) is not completed except by frightening, and the frightening is not fully beneficial except by bringing that thing into existence, it becomes necessary to bring that kind of punishment into existence, in order to achieve that aim which is the obligation. However, the first aspect is closer to me, and the evidence for it is that He said after it: ﴿O My servants, so fear Me﴾, and His saying ﴿O My servants﴾ most clearly indicates that what is meant is the believers. So it is as if it were said: the purpose of describing the punishment of the disbelievers to the believers is to frighten the believers, so O believers, exert yourselves in fear, caution and piety.

When Allah explained their loss, He described that loss with the utmost horribleness, saying: ﴿Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss﴾, so the repetition was for the sake of emphasis.

**The third:** the word ﴿*huwa*﴾ (it) in His saying ﴿It is the manifest loss﴾ implies exclusivity, as if it were said: every loss, when set against it, is as if it were no loss at all.

**The fourth:** describing it as ﴿manifest﴾ indicates awe-inspiring severity. I say: We have already explained that the wording of the verse indicates that it is a manifest loss, so let us now clarify, according to rational investigations, that it is a manifest loss. I say: we need to explain two matters: that it is a loss, and then that it is manifest. As for the first, its explanation is that He, exalted, gave this life, gave the intellect, and gave capacity, and all of that is the capital. As for this life, its purpose is that one may acquire within it a good life in the Hereafter.

* * *

As for the intellect, it is an expression for the self-evident knowledge, and this self-evident knowledge is the capital. Reflection and thinking have no meaning except arranging knowledge so that through that arrangement one may reach the acquisition of acquired knowledge. Thus, that self-evident knowledge called the intellect is the capital, and its composition in specific ways resembles the merchant's handling of his capital, and its composition in ways of buying and selling. The attainment of knowledge of the conclusion resembles the attainment of profit. Likewise, the attainment of the capacity for deeds resembles the capital, and the use of that power in attaining deeds of righteousness and goodness resembles the merchant's handling of his capital, and the attainment of deeds of righteousness and goodness resembles profit. Once this is established, we say: whoever Allah has given life, intellect and capacity, and then he has not benefited from them either the knowledge of the truth or the performance of good at all, he has been deprived of profit entirely, and when he dies the capital is wholly lost, and that is a loss. This is the explanation of its being a loss.

As for the second, which is the explanation that this loss is manifest: whoever does not gain an increase, but nonetheless is safe from calamities and harms, then just as he has not obtained an additional benefit, he has also not obtained an additional harm. As for these disbelievers, they have used their intellects, which are their capital, in extracting the aspects of doubts and strengthening ignorance and misguidance, and they have used their powers and capacities in deeds of evil, falsehood and corruption. Thus they have combined matters that are in the utmost baseness:

First: they have exhausted their bodies and their intellects in seeking those false beliefs and corrupt deeds.

Second: when they die, the capital is lost from them without any benefit.

Third: those severe hardships that existed in the world in support of those misguidances become causes for severe punishment and great affliction after death. Upon reflecting on these meanings, it becomes clear that no loss can be conceived that is greater than their loss, nor any deprivation greater than their deprivation, and we seek refuge in Allah from it.

What is meant is the encompassing of the Fire around them from all sides, and its parallel in the inner states is the encompassing of ignorance, deprivation, greed and all the blameworthy traits around a person. If it is asked: the *ẓulal* (layers) are what is above a person, so how is what is beneath him called *ẓulal*? The answer has several aspects:

The first: it is from the category of applying the name of one of two opposites to the other, like His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40].

The second: that which is beneath a person becomes a layer (*ẓulla*) for another person beneath him, because the Fire has degrees (*darakāt*) just as Paradise has ranks (*darajāt*).

The third: when the lower layer resembles the upper layer in heat, burning and harm, the name of one of them is applied to the other because of similarity and resemblance.

A parallel to this verse is His exalted saying: ﴿On the Day the punishment will cover them from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 55], and His exalted saying: ﴿For them from Hell is a bed, and above them are coverings﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 41].

The first: the meaning is: that punishment prepared for the disbelievers is what Allah threatens His servants with, i.e., the believers, because we have explained that the word *ʿibād* (servants) in the Qur'an is specific to the people of faith.
