Know that when He, may He be exalted, explained the negation of equality between those who know and those who do not know, He followed it by commanding His Messenger to address the believers with various kinds of speech:

The first kind: His saying: ﴿Say: O My servants who have believed, fear your Lord.﴾ The meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, commanded the believers to add taqwa (God-consciousness) to faith. This is among the first proofs that faith remains alongside disobedience. The judge (al-Qadi) said: He commanded them to taqwa so that they would not nullify their faith, because when they guard against major sins their reward remains safe for them, and by committing them it is nullified. It is said to him: this indicates the opposite of your claim is more appropriate, because when He commanded the believers to taqwa, that indicates that they remain believers in the absence of taqwa, and that indicates that immorality does not remove faith.

Know that when He, exalted is He, commanded the believers to guard themselves, He explained to them the benefits of this guarding, so He said: ﴿For those who do good in this world there is good.﴾ His saying ﴿in this world﴾ may be connected either to His saying ﴿do good﴾ or to "good." On the first reading, its meaning is: for those who do good in this world, all of them, there is good in the Hereafter, which is entry into Paradise. The indefiniteness in His saying ﴿good﴾ is for magnification, meaning: a good beyond which the intellect cannot reach the full reality of its perfection.

As for the second reading, its meaning is: those who do good, for them in this world there is good. Those who hold this view said: this good is health and well-being. I say: it is better to interpret it as the three mentioned in his saying ﴿ﷺ﴾: "Three things have no limit: security, health, and sufficiency." Some people said: the first view is more appropriate, and this is supported by several considerations:

The first: the indefiniteness in His saying ﴿good﴾ indicates supremacy, exaltedness and loftiness, which does not befit the conditions of this world, for it is lowly and transient, but befits the conditions of the Hereafter, for it is noble and safe from ending and perishing.

The second: the reward of the one who does good through monotheism and righteous deeds is only obtained in the Hereafter. He, exalted, said: ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned﴾ [Ghafir: 17]. Also, the worldly blessings of health, security and sufficiency are obtained by the disbelievers too. Moreover, their attainment by the disbeliever is greater and more complete than their attainment by the believer, as he ﷺ said: "This world is a prison for the believer and a paradise for the disbeliever." And He, exalted, said: ﴿Had We not feared that people would become one community, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver roofs for their houses and stairways by which they ascend﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 33].

The third: His saying ﴿For those who do good in this world there is good﴾ conveys restriction, meaning that the good of this world is attained only by those who do good. This is false. But if we take this good as the good of the Hereafter, this restriction is valid. Thus interpreting it as the good of the Hereafter is more appropriate. Then Allah, exalted, said: ﴿And the earth of Allah is spacious,﴾ and concerning it there are two views:

The first: the meaning is that there is absolutely no excuse for those who fall short in doing good, even if they plead their homelands and countries, and that they cannot devote themselves to doing good and directing their resolve toward it there. Say to them: indeed the earth of Allah is spacious and His lands are many, so migrate from these lands to lands where you can be occupied with acts of obedience and worship, and follow the examples of the prophets and righteous ones

in their migration to other than their lands, so that they may increase in good upon their good and in obedience upon their obedience. The intended purpose is encouragement to migrate from Makkah to Madinah and patience upon leaving the homeland. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿They said, "In what were you?" They said, "We were oppressed in the land." They said, "Was not the earth of Allah spacious, so that you could emigrate therein?"﴾ [An-Nisa: 97].

The second view: Abu Muslim said: it is not impossible that the intended meaning of "the earth" is the earth of Paradise. This is because He, exalted, commanded the believers to taqwa, which is fear of Allah, then explained that whoever is God-conscious, for him in the Hereafter is good, which is eternal abiding in Paradise. Then He explained that the earth of Allah, that is His Paradise, is spacious, due to His saying: ﴿We shall settle in Paradise wherever we will﴾ [Az-Zumar: 74], and His saying: ﴿A Paradise whose width is the heavens and the earth, prepared for the righteous﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133]. But the first view is preferable to me, because His saying ﴿Indeed, those who are patient will be given their reward without account﴾ befits only the first.

In this verse there are issues:

* * *

First issue: As for the detailed discussion of the reality of patience, we have mentioned it in Surat al-Baqarah. The intended meaning here by "the patient" is those who were patient in leaving their homelands and kin, in swallowing bitter draughts, and in bearing trials in obedience to Allah, exalted is He.

Second issue: Calling the benefits that Allah promised for patience a "reward" may give the impression that the deed earns the reward, since reward is what is deserved. However, decisive proofs establish that the deed does not make reward obligatory, so the word "reward" must be taken as a reward according to the promise, not according to entitlement.

Third issue: He, exalted, described that reward as "without account," and concerning this there are several views:

The first: al-Jubba'i said: the meaning is that they are given what they deserve and more by way of bounty, so it is "without account." Had they been given only what they deserved, that would have been an account. The judge (al-Qadi) said: this is not correct, because Allah, exalted, described the reward as "without account," and even if they were given only the reward they deserve, the reward is other than bounty.

The second: the reward has three attributes:
One: that it is a perpetual reward for them. His saying ﴿without account﴾ means without end, because everything that falls under account is finite, so what has no end is outside account.
Second: that its benefits are complete in themselves, and the intellect of the obedient one could never reach the full reality of that reward. He ﷺ said: "In Paradise there is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." Every kind of reward they witness they find greater than what they imagined and expected, and what a person does not expect may be said to be not within his reckoning. So His saying ﴿without account﴾ is taken in this sense. The third interpretation is that the reward of the people of trial cannot be measured by balance or measure. Ṣāḥib al-Kashshaf narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "On the Day of Resurrection Allah will set up the scales. The people of prayer will come and their rewards will be weighed out for them by the scales, and the people of charity will come and their rewards will be weighed out for them by the scales, and the people of trial will come, and no scale will be set up for them nor any register unfolded for them, and reward will be poured out upon them in a torrent." Allah, exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who are patient will be given their reward without account,﴾ so that the people of well-being in this world wish that their bodies were cut with shears because of the excellence the people of trial have.

The second kind of the explanations which Allah commanded His Messenger to mention is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion.﴾ Muqatil said: The disbelievers of Quraysh said to the Prophet ﷺ: "What drives you to this religion which you have brought us? Do you not look at the religion of your father and grandfather and the leaders of your people, who worship al-Lat and al-'Uzza?" So Allah revealed: "Say, O Muhammad, indeed I have been commanded to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion."

I say: Obligation is of two kinds:
One of them: the command to refrain from what is not fitting.
The second: the command to attain what is fitting. The first level takes precedence over the second according to the necessary, binding rank. Having established this, we say: He, exalted, placed first the command to remove what is not fitting, saying ﴿fear your Lord﴾, because taqwa is refraining from what is not fitting. Then immediately after it He mentioned the command to attain what is fitting, saying ﴿Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion.﴾ This comprises two conditions:
One: the command to worship Allah.
Second: that this worship be free from the taints of overt shirk and the taints of hidden shirk. Allah, exalted, specified the Messenger with this command in order to alert that others are more entitled to it; so it is like an encouragement to others. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims﴾ undoubtedly means: I am the first to adhere to the acts of worship with which I was sent. In this verse there are two benefits:

The first benefit: it is as if he says: I am not one of the tyrannical kings who command people to things they themselves do not do; rather, everything I have commanded you to do, I am the first of people to begin it and the most constant in it.

The second benefit: He said ﴿I have been commanded to worship Allah﴾, and worship has two pillars: the work of the heart and the work of the limbs. The work of the heart is more noble than the work of the limbs, so He mentioned first the nobler part, which is His saying ﴿being sincere to Him in religion﴾, then immediately after it mentioned the lesser, which is the work of the limbs, namely Islam, for the Prophet ﷺ explained Islam in the report about Jibril, peace be upon him, as the outward deeds, and this is what is meant by His saying in this verse: ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims.﴾ Nor may anyone say: what is the benefit of repeating the word "commanded"? We answer: the word "commanded" is mentioned first with the work of the heart and second with the work of the limbs, so this is not repetition.

The third benefit in His saying ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims﴾ is an alert that being a Messenger from Allah is obligatory to obey, because the first of the Muslims in the laws of Allah can only be the Messenger of Allah, since the first to know those laws and obligations is the Messenger who conveys them. When Allah, exalted, clarified his command to sincerity in the heart and to the specific deeds, and the command may admit of obligation or recommendation, He clarified that this command is for obligation, so He said: ﴿Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great day.﴾ In this there are benefits:

The first benefit: Allah commanded Muhammad ﷺ to apply this statement to himself, and the purpose is to intensify the warning to others against sins, for if, despite his great rank and the nobility of his prophethood, he must be fearful and wary of sins, then others are more deserving of that.

The second benefit: the verse indicates that what is entailed by disobedience is not the occurrence of punishment but fear of punishment. This accords with our statement that Allah, exalted, may pardon the sinner and the major sin, so the necessary consequence upon the occurrence of disobedience is fear of punishment, not the actual occurrence of punishment.

The third benefit: this verse indicates that the apparent meaning of a command is obligation, because He said at the beginning of the verse: ﴿Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah,﴾ then after it said: ﴿Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great day.﴾ So the meaning of this disobedience is abandoning the command mentioned earlier, and this requires that one who abandons the command is disobedient, and the disobedient is subject to fear of punishment, and there is no meaning of obligation except that.

Page 223

**The third type of thing that Allah commanded His Messenger to mention is His saying:** ﴿Say: It is Allah I worship, sincere in my religion to Him.﴾ If it is asked: what is the meaning of the repetition in His saying ﴿Say: I have been commanded to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ and His saying ﴿Say: It is Allah I worship, sincere in my religion to Him﴾? We say: this is not a repetition, because the first is an informing that he is commanded by Allah to perform worship, and the second is an informing that he was commanded not to worship anyone other than Him. This is because His saying ﴿I have been commanded to worship Allah﴾ does not imply exclusivity (*hasr*), whereas His exalted saying ﴿It is Allah I worship﴾ does imply exclusivity, meaning: I worship Allah and do not worship anyone besides Him. The evidence for this is that after He said ﴿It is Allah I worship﴾, He said after it: ﴿Worship what you will besides Him﴾. There is no doubt that His saying ﴿Worship what you will besides Him﴾ is not a command, but rather its purpose is a rebuke (*zajr*), as if He is saying: since the clarification regarding the obligation of upholding monotheism has reached its utmost limit, then after this you are more knowledgeable about yourselves. Then He explained the completeness of the rebuke with His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed the losers are those who have lost themselves﴾, because of their falling into a destruction beyond which no destruction can be conceived, ﴿and their families [as well]﴾, because if they are among the people of the Fire, they have lost them just as they lost themselves, and if they are among the people of Paradise, they have departed from them with a departure after which there is absolutely no return. Ibn ʿAbbas said: indeed every man has a dwelling, a family and servants in Paradise; if he obeys, he is given that, and if he is among the people of the Fire, he is deprived of that, so he has lost his self, his family and his dwelling, and others among the Muslims inherit it. The *khasir* (loser) is the one who is defrauded. When Allah explained their loss, He described that loss with the utmost horribleness, saying: ﴿Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss﴾, so the repetition was for the sake of emphasis.

**The second:** He, exalted, mentioned at the beginning of this statement the particle ﴿*alā*﴾ (unquestionably), which is for alerting, and mentioning alerting in this place indicates magnification, as if it were said: He has reached such greatness that your minds cannot attain to it, so be alert to it.

**The third:** the word ﴿*huwa*﴾ (it) in His saying ﴿It is the manifest loss﴾ implies exclusivity, as if it were said: every loss, when set against it, is as if it were no loss at all.

**The fourth:** describing it as ﴿manifest﴾ indicates awe-inspiring severity. I say: We have already explained that the wording of the verse indicates that it is a manifest loss, so let us now clarify, according to rational investigations, that it is a manifest loss. I say: we need to explain two matters: that it is a loss, and then that it is manifest. As for the first, its explanation is that He, exalted, gave this life, gave the intellect, and gave capacity, and all of that is the capital. As for this life, its purpose is that one may acquire within it a good life in the Hereafter.

* * *

As for the intellect, it is an expression for the self-evident knowledge, and this self-evident knowledge is the capital. Reflection and thinking have no meaning except arranging knowledge so that through that arrangement one may reach the acquisition of acquired knowledge. Thus, that self-evident knowledge called the intellect is the capital, and its composition in specific ways resembles the merchant's handling of his capital, and its composition in ways of buying and selling. The attainment of knowledge of the conclusion resembles the attainment of profit. Likewise, the attainment of the capacity for deeds resembles the capital, and the use of that power in attaining deeds of righteousness and goodness resembles the merchant's handling of his capital, and the attainment of deeds of righteousness and goodness resembles profit. Once this is established, we say: whoever Allah has given life, intellect and capacity, and then he has not benefited from them either the knowledge of the truth or the performance of good at all, he has been deprived of profit entirely, and when he dies the capital is wholly lost, and that is a loss. This is the explanation of its being a loss.

As for the second, which is the explanation that this loss is manifest: whoever does not gain an increase, but nonetheless is safe from calamities and harms, then just as he has not obtained an additional benefit, he has also not obtained an additional harm. As for these disbelievers, they have used their intellects, which are their capital, in extracting the aspects of doubts and strengthening ignorance and misguidance, and they have used their powers and capacities in deeds of evil, falsehood and corruption. Thus they have combined matters that are in the utmost baseness:

First: they have exhausted their bodies and their intellects in seeking those false beliefs and corrupt deeds.

[p. 224]

Second: when they die, the capital is lost from them without any benefit.

Third: those severe hardships that existed in the world in support of those misguidances become causes for severe punishment and great affliction after death. Upon reflecting on these meanings, it becomes clear that no loss can be conceived that is greater than their loss, nor any deprivation greater than their deprivation, and we seek refuge in Allah from it.

When Allah, exalted, explained the states of their deprivation from profit and clarified the manner of their loss, He made clear that they did not limit themselves to deprivation and loss, but added to it the deserving of a great punishment and a severe retribution, so He said: ﴿For them there will be layers of fire above them and layers below﴾. What is meant is the encompassing of the Fire around them from all sides, and its parallel in the inner states is the encompassing of ignorance, deprivation, greed and all the blameworthy traits around a person. If it is asked: the *ẓulal* (layers) are what is above a person, so how is what is beneath him called *ẓulal*? The answer has several aspects:

The first: it is from the category of applying the name of one of two opposites to the other, like His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40].

The second: that which is beneath a person becomes a layer (*ẓulla*) for another person beneath him, because the Fire has degrees (*darakāt*) just as Paradise has ranks (*darajāt*).

The third: when the lower layer resembles the upper layer in heat, burning and harm, the name of one of them is applied to the other because of similarity and resemblance.

Al-Hasan said: they are between two layers of the Fire, not knowing what is above them more than what is beneath them. A parallel to this verse is His exalted saying: ﴿On the Day the punishment will cover them from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 55], and His exalted saying: ﴿For them from Hell is a bed, and above them are coverings﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 41].

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿This is what Allah threatens His servants with﴾, that is, that which has been mentioned previously of the description of the punishment. So His saying ﴿This﴾ is the subject, and His saying ﴿Allah threatens His servants with it﴾ is the predicate. Regarding His saying ﴿Allah threatens His servants with it﴾ there are two opinions:

The first: the meaning is: that punishment prepared for the disbelievers is what Allah threatens His servants with, i.e., the believers, because we have explained that the word *ʿibād* (servants) in the Qur'an is specific to the people of faith. It was a threat to the believers because when they hear that the state of the disbelievers is as has been mentioned, they fear, and so they become sincere in monotheism and obedience.

The second aspect: this statement is in the form of an answer to a question, because it may be said: He, exalted, is independent of the worlds, free of desire, vengeance and the motive to harm, so how is it fitting for Him to punish these wretched people to this great extent? The answer to this is that the purpose of it is to frighten the disbelievers and the misguided away from disbelief and misguidance. When obligation (*taklīf*) is not completed except by frightening, and the frightening is not fully beneficial except by bringing that thing into existence, it becomes necessary to bring that kind of punishment into existence, in order to achieve that aim which is the obligation. However, the first aspect is closer to me, and the evidence for it is that He said after it: ﴿O My servants, so fear Me﴾, and His saying ﴿O My servants﴾ most clearly indicates that what is meant is the believers. So it is as if it were said: the purpose of describing the punishment of the disbelievers to the believers is to frighten the believers, so O believers, exert yourselves in fear, caution and piety.

Allah, exalted, specified the Messenger with this command in order to alert that others are more entitled to it; so it is like an encouragement to others. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims﴾ undoubtedly means: I am the first to adhere to the acts of worship with which I was sent. In this verse there are two benefits:

The first benefit: it is as if he says: I am not one of the tyrannical kings who command people to things they themselves do not do; rather, everything I have commanded you to do, I am the first of people to begin it and the most constant in it.

The second benefit: He said ﴿I have been commanded to worship Allah﴾, and worship has two pillars: the work of the heart and the work of the limbs. The work of the heart is more noble than the work of the limbs, so He mentioned first the nobler part, which is His saying ﴿being sincere to Him in religion﴾, then immediately after it mentioned the lesser, which is the work of the limbs, namely Islam, for the Prophet ﷺ explained Islam in the report about Jibril, peace be upon him, as the outward deeds, and this is what is meant by His saying in this verse: ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims.﴾ Nor may anyone say: what is the benefit of repeating the word "commanded"? We answer: the word "commanded" is mentioned first with the work of the heart and second with the work of the limbs, so this is not repetition.

The third benefit in His saying ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims﴾ is an alert that being a Messenger from Allah is obligatory to obey, because the first of the Muslims in the laws of Allah can only be the Messenger of Allah, since the first to know those laws and obligations is the Messenger who conveys them. When Allah, exalted, clarified his command to sincerity in the heart and to the specific deeds, and the command may admit of obligation or recommendation, He clarified that this command is for obligation, so He said: ﴿Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great day.﴾ In this there are benefits:

The first benefit: Allah commanded Muhammad ﷺ to apply this statement to himself, and the purpose is to intensify the warning to others against sins, for if, despite his great rank and the nobility of his prophethood, he must be fearful and wary of sins, then others are more deserving of that.

The second benefit: the verse indicates that what is entailed by disobedience is not the occurrence of punishment but fear of punishment. This accords with our statement that Allah, exalted, may pardon the sinner and the major sin, so the necessary consequence upon the occurrence of disobedience is fear of punishment, not the actual occurrence of punishment.

The third benefit: this verse indicates that the apparent meaning of a command is obligation, because He said at the beginning of the verse: ﴿Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah,﴾ then after it said: ﴿Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great day.﴾ So the meaning of this disobedience is abandoning the command mentioned earlier, and this requires that one who abandons the command is disobedient, and the disobedient is subject to fear of punishment, and there is no meaning of obligation except that.

Page 223

**The third type of thing that Allah commanded His Messenger to mention is His saying:** ﴿Say: It is Allah I worship, sincere in my religion to Him.﴾ If it is asked: what is the meaning of the repetition in His saying ﴿Say: I have been commanded to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ and His saying ﴿Say: It is Allah I worship, sincere in my religion to Him﴾? We say: this is not a repetition, because the first is an informing that he is commanded by Allah to perform worship, and the second is an informing that he was commanded not to worship anyone other than Him. This is because His saying ﴿I have been commanded to worship Allah﴾ does not imply exclusivity (*hasr*), whereas His exalted saying ﴿It is Allah I worship﴾ does imply exclusivity, meaning: I worship Allah and do not worship anyone besides Him. The evidence for this is that after He said ﴿It is Allah I worship﴾, He said after it: ﴿Worship what you will besides Him﴾. There is no doubt that His saying ﴿Worship what you will besides Him﴾ is not a command, but rather its purpose is a rebuke (*zajr*), as if He is saying: since the clarification regarding the obligation of upholding monotheism has reached its utmost limit, then after this you are more knowledgeable about yourselves. Then He explained the completeness of the rebuke with His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed the losers are those who have lost themselves﴾, because of their falling into a destruction beyond which no destruction can be conceived, ﴿and their families [as well]﴾, because if they are among the people of the Fire, they have lost them just as they lost themselves, and if they are among the people of Paradise, they have departed from them with a departure after which there is absolutely no return. Ibn ʿAbbas said: indeed every man has a dwelling, a family and servants in Paradise; if he obeys, he is given that, and if he is among the people of the Fire, he is deprived of that, so he has lost his self, his family and his dwelling, and others among the Muslims inherit it. The *khasir* (loser) is the one who is defrauded. When Allah explained their loss, He described that loss with the utmost horribleness, saying: ﴿Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss﴾, so the repetition was for the sake of emphasis.

**The second:** He, exalted, mentioned at the beginning of this statement the particle ﴿*alā*﴾ (unquestionably), which is for alerting, and mentioning alerting in this place indicates magnification, as if it were said: He has reached such greatness that your minds cannot attain to it, so be alert to it.

**The third:** the word ﴿*huwa*﴾ (it) in His saying ﴿It is the manifest loss﴾ implies exclusivity, as if it were said: every loss, when set against it, is as if it were no loss at all.

**The fourth:** describing it as ﴿manifest﴾ indicates awe-inspiring severity. I say: We have already explained that the wording of the verse indicates that it is a manifest loss, so let us now clarify, according to rational investigations, that it is a manifest loss. I say: we need to explain two matters: that it is a loss, and then that it is manifest. As for the first, its explanation is that He, exalted, gave this life, gave the intellect, and gave capacity, and all of that is the capital. As for this life, its purpose is that one may acquire within it a good life in the Hereafter.

* * *

As for the intellect, it is an expression for the self-evident knowledge, and this self-evident knowledge is the capital. Reflection and thinking have no meaning except arranging knowledge so that through that arrangement one may reach the acquisition of acquired knowledge. Thus, that self-evident knowledge called the intellect is the capital, and its composition in specific ways resembles the merchant's handling of his capital, and its composition in ways of buying and selling. The attainment of knowledge of the conclusion resembles the attainment of profit. Likewise, the attainment of the capacity for deeds resembles the capital, and the use of that power in attaining deeds of righteousness and goodness resembles the merchant's handling of his capital, and the attainment of deeds of righteousness and goodness resembles profit. Once this is established, we say: whoever Allah has given life, intellect and capacity, and then he has not benefited from them either the knowledge of the truth or the performance of good at all, he has been deprived of profit entirely, and when he dies the capital is wholly lost, and that is a loss. This is the explanation of its being a loss.

As for the second, which is the explanation that this loss is manifest: whoever does not gain an increase, but nonetheless is safe from calamities and harms, then just as he has not obtained an additional benefit, he has also not obtained an additional harm. As for these disbelievers, they have used their intellects, which are their capital, in extracting the aspects of doubts and strengthening ignorance and misguidance, and they have used their powers and capacities in deeds of evil, falsehood and corruption. Thus they have combined matters that are in the utmost baseness:

First: they have exhausted their bodies and their intellects in seeking those false beliefs and corrupt deeds.

[p. 224]

Second: when they die, the capital is lost from them without any benefit.

Third: those severe hardships that existed in the world in support of those misguidances become causes for severe punishment and great affliction after death. Upon reflecting on these meanings, it becomes clear that no loss can be conceived that is greater than their loss, nor any deprivation greater than their deprivation, and we seek refuge in Allah from it.

When Allah, exalted, explained the states of their deprivation from profit and clarified the manner of their loss, He made clear that they did not limit themselves to deprivation and loss, but added to it the deserving of a great punishment and a severe retribution, so He said: ﴿For them there will be layers of fire above them and layers below﴾. What is meant is the encompassing of the Fire around them from all sides, and its parallel in the inner states is the encompassing of ignorance, deprivation, greed and all the blameworthy traits around a person. If it is asked: the *ẓulal* (layers) are what is above a person, so how is what is beneath him called *ẓulal*? The answer has several aspects:

The first: it is from the category of applying the name of one of two opposites to the other, like His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40].

The second: that which is beneath a person becomes a layer (*ẓulla*) for another person beneath him, because the Fire has degrees (*darakāt*) just as Paradise has ranks (*darajāt*).

The third: when the lower layer resembles the upper layer in heat, burning and harm, the name of one of them is applied to the other because of similarity and resemblance.

Al-Hasan said: they are between two layers of the Fire, not knowing what is above them more than what is beneath them. A parallel to this verse is His exalted saying: ﴿On the Day the punishment will cover them from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 55], and His exalted saying: ﴿For them from Hell is a bed, and above them are coverings﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 41].

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿This is what Allah threatens His servants with﴾, that is, that which has been mentioned previously of the description of the punishment. So His saying ﴿This﴾ is the subject, and His saying ﴿Allah threatens His servants with it﴾ is the predicate. Regarding His saying ﴿Allah threatens His servants with it﴾ there are two opinions:

The first: the meaning is: that punishment prepared for the disbelievers is what Allah threatens His servants with, i.e., the believers, because we have explained that the word *ʿibād* (servants) in the Qur'an is specific to the people of faith. It was a threat to the believers because when they hear that the state of the disbelievers is as has been mentioned, they fear, and so they become sincere in monotheism and obedience.

The second aspect: this statement is in the form of an answer to a question, because it may be said: He, exalted, is independent of the worlds, free of desire, vengeance and the motive to harm, so how is it fitting for Him to punish these wretched people to this great extent? The answer to this is that the purpose of it is to frighten the disbelievers and the misguided away from disbelief and misguidance. When obligation (*taklīf*) is not completed except by frightening, and the frightening is not fully beneficial except by bringing that thing into existence, it becomes necessary to bring that kind of punishment into existence, in order to achieve that aim which is the obligation. However, the first aspect is closer to me, and the evidence for it is that He said after it: ﴿O My servants, so fear Me﴾, and His saying ﴿O My servants﴾ most clearly indicates that what is meant is the believers. So it is as if it were said: the purpose of describing the punishment of the disbelievers to the believers is to frighten the believers, so O believers, exert yourselves in fear, caution and piety.

[Page 225]

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who avoid the Taghut, not worshipping it, and turn back in repentance to Allah, for them is good news. So give good tidings to My servants, ﴿who listen to the word and follow the best of it. Those are the ones Allah has guided, and those are the people of understanding.﴾ ﴿Is one against whom the word of punishment has been decreed [to be saved]? Would you then save one who is in the Fire?﴾ ﴿But those who feared their Lord will have chambers above them, with chambers built above them, beneath which rivers flow. The promise of Allah; Allah does not fail in His promise.﴾**

Know that when Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned the threat against the worshippers of idols and images, He mentioned the promise for those who avoided worshipping them and guarded themselves against shirk, so that the promise would always be paired with the threat, and thereby the full measure of encouragement and warning would be achieved. In this verse there are several issues.

**The first issue:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari's Qur'an commentary) said: *al-Taghut* is on the pattern *fa'lut*, from *al-tughyan* (transgression), like *al-malakut* (sovereignty) and *al-rahamut* (mercy), except that in it there is a metathesis (*qalb*), by placing the lam before the ayn. In this word there are several kinds of intensification:

First: it is named by the verbal noun, as if the very essence of that thing is transgression.

Second: the form is a form of intensification, for *al-rahamut* is vast mercy, and *al-malakut* is extensive dominion.

Third: what we have mentioned, the placing of the lam before the ayn, and such a form is only resorted to for intensification.

**The second issue:** Scholars differed over whether *al-Taghut* here refers to the Devil (*al-Shaytan*) or to the idols (*al-Awthan*). It was said: it is the Devil. If it is said: they did not worship the Devil; they worshipped the idol. We say: the one who calls to the worship of the idol is the Devil, so that undertaking the worship of the idol is worship of the Devil. It was also said: the intended meaning of *al-Taghut* is the idol, and it was called *tawaghit* (plural) by way of metaphor, because it has no action of its own, and the transgressors (*al-tughat*) are those who worship it; but when transgression occurs at the sight of it and in proximity to it, it was described with this attribute, by naming the effect with the name of the cause according to outward appearance. It was also said: everything that is worshipped and obeyed besides Allah is *taghut*. It is related in the historical accounts that the origin of idol worship was that the people were anthropomorphists (*mushabbiha*), who believed about God that He is a great light, and about the angels that they are lights varying in size; so they set up statues and images in accordance with those imaginings, and they worshipped those statues believing that they were worshipping Allah and the angels.

I say: the sum of the statement in His saying, *"And those who avoid the Taghut"*, meaning: they turned away from worshipping everything other than Allah. His saying, *"and turn back in repentance to Allah"*, meaning: they returned wholly to Allah. I found in the Fifth Book of the *Tawrah* (Torah) that Allah, Exalted is He, said to Moses: "O Moses, respond to your God with all your heart."

I say: as long as there remains in the heart any turning toward other than Allah, one has not responded to one's God with all one's heart. Response with the whole heart is achieved only when the heart turns away from everything other than Allah among the means of acts of obedience. How then can one turn away from them, when one perceives with the senses the causes that lead to effects in this world? We say: the intended meaning of the heart's turning away from them is not that one should judge them to be non-existent, for that is entering into sophistry (*al-sufsata*), which is false. Rather, the intended meaning is that one should know that the Necessary Existent in Himself (*wajib al-wujud li-dhatihi*) is One, and that everything other than Him is possible in its own essence (*mumkin al-wujud li-dhatihi*), and everything that is possible in its own essence exists only through the bringing into being and creating of the Necessary. Then, He, glorified and exalted, has made His bringing things into being of two kinds: some of them occur without intermediary, and these are the world of the heavens and the spiritual beings; and some of them occur through intermediary, and this is the world of the elements and the lower world. When you know things in this manner, you know that all belongs to Allah, from Allah, and through Allah, and that there is no manager except Him and no effective agent other than Him. Then his gaze is detached from these possible things, and his heart remains occupied with the First Effector and the First Originator. For if He has set up the spiritual and physical causes in such a way that they lead to this goal, then this thing comes about; and if He has set them up in such a way that they do not lead to the occurrence of this thing, it does not occur. By this path his gaze is detached from all, and no turning of his heart remains toward anything except the existent

[Page 226]

First. It happened that I was advising some young men about guarding honor and wealth, and he opposed me and said: It is not permissible to rely on effort and striving; rather, one must rely on the decree and destiny of Allah. I said: This is a true word you have heard, but you have not understood its meaning. For there is no doubt that everything is from Allah, Exalted is He, but He, glorified is He, has arranged things in two kinds: some of them He made their occurrence and coming into being dependent on known causes, and others He brings into being without the intermediary of these causes.

As for the first kind: it is the events of this lower world.

As for the second kind: it is the events of that higher world. Once this is established, we say: whoever seeks the events of this lower world not from the causes which Allah, Exalted is He, has determined, that person is contending with Allah in His wisdom and opposing His management; for Allah, Exalted is He, has decreed that these things occur on the basis of those specified and known causes, and you want to obtain them not from those causes. This is the discussion in verifying the turning away from other than Allah and the complete turning toward Allah, Exalted is He. Thus His saying, *"And those who avoid the Taghut"*, is an indication of turning away from other than Allah, and His saying, *"and turn back in repentance to Allah"*, is an indication of wholly turning toward the worship of Allah.

Then, Exalted is He, promised these people several things:

The first of them is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿for them is good news﴾.

Know that this word relates to several aspects:

The first: when does this good news occur? We say: it occurs at the approach of death, when placed in the grave, when standing on the plain of Resurrection, when a group is in Paradise and a group in the Blaze, and when the believers enter Paradise. In each of these standing-places, good news occurs with some kind of goodness, spirit, comfort and fragrant provision.

The second: by what does this good news come about? We say: this good news comes about by the removal of what is disliked and by the attainment of what is desired. As for the removal of what is disliked, His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Fear not, nor grieve﴾ [Fussilat: 30]. Fear is only of the future, and grief is only because of past states. So His saying *"Fear not"* means: do not fear what you will face of the states of the Resurrection, and do not grieve over what has escaped you of the good things of this world. When Allah removed these disliked things from them, He gave them good news of the attainment of goods and felicities, and said: ﴿and rejoice in the Garden﴾ [Fussilat: 30]. He also said in another verse: ﴿On the Day you see the believing men and believing women, their light running before them and on their right: "Good news for you today: gardens beneath which rivers flow"﴾ [al-Hadid: 12]. He also said: ﴿Therein is what the souls desire and what the eyes delight in, and you therein will abide forever﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 71].

The third: who is the bringer of good news? We say: it is possibly the angels, either at death, as in His saying: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death, good, saying: "Peace be upon you"﴾ [al-Nahl: 32], or after entering Paradise, as in His saying: ﴿The angels will enter upon them from every gate: "Peace be upon you, for what you patiently endured; how excellent is the final abode!"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 24]. It is possibly Allah Himself, glorified is He, as He said: ﴿Their greeting on the Day they meet Him will be "Peace"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 44].

Know that His saying, *"for them is good news"*, contains several kinds of emphasis:

First: it implies restriction (*al-hasr*). His saying *"for them is good news"* means: for them and not for others. This indicates that there is no good news for anyone unless he avoids worshipping other than Allah, Exalted is He, and turns wholly toward Allah, Exalted is He.

Second: the definite article in the word *"al-bushra"* (the good news) indicates the reality (*al-mahiyya*), so it indicates that this reality in its entirety belongs to these people, and no share of it remains for others.

Third: there is no difference between information (*al-ikhbar*) and good news (*al-bishara*); good news is the first report of the attainment of goods. Knowing this, we say: all the kinds of reward and good that they heard about in this world, when they hear it at death or in the grave, that is not but information. Thus it is established that this good news is not realized except when information is given of the attainment of other kinds of felicities beyond what they knew and heard of in this world. We ask Allah, Exalted is He, for success in attaining them. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿No soul knows what is hidden for them of the delight of the eyes﴾ [al-Sajda: 17].

Fourth: the one who informs by His saying *"for them is good news"* is Allah, Exalted is He, the Greatest of the great and the most perfect of existents. The condition required for the attainment of this good news is a great condition, namely avoiding what is other than Allah, Exalted is He, and turning wholly toward Allah. When a great sovereign mentions a great condition, then says to one who has fulfilled that great condition: "Rejoice," this good news issuing from the great sovereign, conditioned on the fulfilment of that great condition, indicates that the thing of which the good news is given has reached such a degree of perfection and elevation that minds and thoughts cannot reach its description. Thus it is established that His saying *"for them is good news"* indicates the utmost perfection and felicity in these respects. And Allah knows best.

Know that when He, Exalted is He, said *"for them is good news"*, and this was a general statement, He followed it with a statement which serves as an explanation and elaboration of it, so He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So give good tidings to My servants, who listen to the word and follow the best of it﴾. By "My servants, who listen to the word and follow the best of it," He meant those who avoided and turned back, and no others. This indicates that the head of felicities, the center of goods, and the source of honors is turning away from other than Allah, Exalted is He, and wholly turning toward obedience to Allah. The purpose of this expression is to draw attention to the fact that those who avoided the Taghut and turned back are the ones described as "those who listen to the word and follow the best of it." Thus the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, to draw attention to this point. Some have said: when He, Exalted is He, made clear that those who avoided and turned back have good news, and that this was a high rank which only the foremost attain, and restricting felicity to them implies deprivation for the majority, which does not befit complete mercy, He therefore made the ruling more general, and said: whoever chooses the best in every matter is among the company of the fortunate. Know that this verse indicates several benefits.

* * *

**The first benefit:** the obligation of reflection and reasoning (*al-nazar wa-al-istidlal*). This is because He, Exalted is He, has made clear that guidance and success are linked to a person hearing many things, from which he chooses what is best and most correct. It is known that distinguishing the best and most correct from other things is not attained by hearing alone, because hearing has become a common ground shared by all; for His saying *"who listen to the word"* indicates that hearing is a common quality in which all participate. Thus it is established that distinguishing the best from other things is not achieved by hearing, but is achieved by the proof of reason (*hujjat al-'aql*). This indicates that what necessitates deserving praise and commendation is following the proof of reason, and building the matter upon reflection and reasoning.

**The second benefit:** the paths to establishing the correctness of doctrines and religions are of two kinds:

One of them: establishing the argument and the clear evidence for its soundness by way of acquiring knowledge (*al-tahsil*), and this is something that cannot be attained except by delving into each of the issues in detail.

The second point: before we investigate the proofs, state them, and refute the doubts about them, we present these doctrines and their opposites to our intellects. Whichever doctrine the intellect first judges to be better and more perfect deserves to be accepted more. An example: clear reason testifies that affirming that the God of the world is living, knowing, powerful, forbearing, wise and merciful is better than denying it, so that doctrine is the better one. Likewise, affirming that God Most High does not bring about in His dominion and authority anything except what accords with His will is better than saying that most of what occurs in God's authority is contrary to His will. Also, affirming that God is one, unique, self-sufficient, and free from composition and parts is better than saying He is divisible and composite. Also, saying that He is independent of time and place is better than saying He needs them. Also, saying that God is merciful and generous and may pardon punishment is better than saying that He never pardons it at all. All these matters fall under His saying: ﴿Those who listen to the word and follow the best of it﴾. This is what pertains to choosing the best in matters of belief.

As for what pertains to the matters of obligations (al-takalif), it is of two kinds: some of them are among the acts of worship ('ibadat), and some are among the transactions (mu'amalat). As for acts of worship, an example is our saying: the prayer (salah), in which one says at its opening "Allahu akbar," the intention accompanies the takbir, al-Fatihah is recited in it, tranquility is observed in its five positions, the tashahhud is recited in it, and one exits it by saying "al-salamu 'alaykum." Undoubtedly it is better than a prayer in which none of these conditions is observed, and it obliges the rational person to choose this prayer and leave whatever else there is. The same holds for all the acts of worship.

As for transactions, it is likewise. For example, God Most High legislated retaliation (qisas), blood-money (diyah) and pardon, but He encouraged pardon, saying: ﴿And that you pardon is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237]. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that what is meant by it is a man who sits with a people and hears a discourse containing both good and bad, so he relates the best of what he heard and leaves aside the rest.

* * *

Know that God Most High judged those who listen to the word and follow its best by saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom God has guided, and those are the people of understanding﴾. In this there is a wondrous subtlety: the attainment of guidance in the intellect and the spirit is a contingent matter, and it necessarily requires an agent and a recipient. As for the agent, it is God, glorified is He, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom God has guided﴾. As for the recipient, it is indicated by His saying: ﴿and those are the people of understanding﴾, for a person who is not an intellect of complete comprehension cannot have these true cognitions attained in his heart. We have said that the agent of this guidance is God because the substance of the soul, together with the light of intellect that is in it, is receptive to both true belief and false belief. When a thing is receptive to two opposites, its relation to both is equal, and when this is so, it is impossible for that receptive thing to be the cause of the preponderance of one of the two sides. Do you not see that when a body is receptive to motion and rest equally, it is impossible for the very essence of the body to be the cause of the preponderance of one of the two sides over the other? If they say: "We do not say that the essence of the soul and the intellect necessitates this preponderance; rather, we say that it wills to attain one of the two sides, and that volition becomes the cause of that preponderance," we say: this is false, because just as the essence of the soul is receptive to this volition, so too the essence of the intellect is receptive to a volition opposed to that volition. Hence it is impossible for the substance of the soul to be the cause of that volition. Thus it is established that the attainment of guidance necessarily requires an agent and a recipient.

As for the agent: it is impossible that it be the soul itself; rather the agent is God Most High. As for the recipient: it is the substance of the soul. For this reason He said: ﴿Those are the ones whom God has guided, and those are the people of understanding﴾. Then He said: ﴿Then is he who has been justified the word of punishment [to be] one you could save who is in the Fire?﴾ In this there are several issues.

The first issue: in the wording of the verse there is a question, namely that it is said: He said ﴿Then is he who has been justified the word of punishment﴾, and in Arabic speech it is not correct for the interrogative particle to enter both upon the subject and upon the predicate together. One does not say: "Is Zayd, do you kill him?" Rather, here there is something else: just as the interrogative particle enters upon the condition and upon the consequent, so too the particle fa' enters upon both of them together, namely His saying ﴿Then is he who has been justified﴾ and ﴿then can you save﴾. On account of this question, the grammarians differed and mentioned several views concerning it:

The first: al-Kisa'i said: the verse is two sentences, and the implied meaning is: "Then is he upon whom the word of punishment has been justified [to be guided]? Then can you protect him? Then can you save those in the Fire?"

The second: the author of al-Kashshaf said: the original of the speech is: "Then is he upon whom the word of punishment has been justified—then can you save him?" This is a conditional sentence into which the interrogative hamzah of denunciation (inkar) has entered, and the fa' is the fa' of the consequent. Then the fa' that is at its beginning entered for coordination upon an omitted element indicated by the address, and the implied meaning is: "Are you the master of their affair? Then he upon whom the word of punishment has been justified—then can you save him?" The second hamzah is the first one, repeated to emphasize the meaning of denunciation and remoteness. "Those in the Fire" was placed in the position of the pronoun, and the verse on this view is a single sentence.

The third: it is not far-fetched to say that the interrogative particle has come here only to convey the meaning of denunciation. And since his denunciation of this meaning is complete and perfect, he has therefore mentioned this particle in the condition and repeated it in the consequent, as a warning to the utmost perfection of that denunciation.

The second issue: the companions (al-Ashab, i.e., the Ash'aris) argued by this verse in the matter of guidance and misguidance. This is because He Most High said: ﴿Then is he who has been justified the word of punishment﴾. When the word of punishment has been justified against him, it is impossible for him to perform faith and obedience, for otherwise it would entail the reversal of God's true report into falsehood and the reversal of His knowledge into ignorance, and that is impossible.

The second way of deriving proof from the verse: He Most High judged that the actuality of the word of punishment necessitates a complete denunciation of the emergence of faith and obedience from him. And if that were possible, and the actuality of the word of punishment were not preventing it, there would remain no meaning to this denunciation and remoteness.

The third issue: the Qadi (al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar) argued by this verse that the Prophet (ﷺ) does not intercede for the people of the major sins. He said: because the punishment has been justified against them, that intercession would function as rescuing them from the Fire, and God Most High has judged against them with denunciation and remoteness. It is said to him: we do not concede that the people of major sins have had the punishment justified against them. And how could punishment be justified against them when God Most High said: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48], and with His saying: ﴿Indeed, God forgives all sins﴾ [al-Zumar: 53]. And God knows best.

The second kind of the things that God promised to those who avoided [false gods] and turned in repentance is His saying: ﴿But those who feared their Lord will have chambers above which are built chambers﴾. This is as a counterpart to what was mentioned in the description of the disbelievers: ﴿For them there will be canopies of fire above them and canopies beneath them﴾. If it is asked: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿built﴾? We answer: because when a dwelling is built upon another dwelling beneath it, the upper one is weaker in construction than the lower one. So His saying ﴿built﴾ means that although it is above others, it is equal in strength and firmness to the lower dwelling. The summary is that both the upper and the lower dwelling have in each of them a virtue and a deficiency: as for the upper, its virtue is height and elevation, and its deficiency is fragility and flimsiness; as for the lower, it is the opposite of this. As for the dwellings of Paradise, they combine all virtues: they are lofty and elevated, and they are in the utmost strength and firmness. The wise men of Islam (hukama' al-Islam) said: these built chambers, some of them above others, have as an example among states of the soul the acquired sciences, for some of them are built upon others; and the final results, which are an expression of knowing the essence of God and His attributes, are in the utmost strength—indeed they are in strength and firmness like the primary, self-evident sciences.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Rivers flow beneath them﴾, which is well known. Then He concluded the speech by saying: ﴿God's promise. God does not fail in His promise﴾. His saying ﴿God's promise﴾ is an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkad), because His saying ﴿for them are chambers﴾ means: God promised them that. In the verse there is a noble subtlety: in many verses of promise He Most High has explicitly stated that this is God's promise and that He does not break His promise, whereas in verses of threat He never mentioned such emphasis and reinforcement at all. This indicates that the side of promise is weightier than the side of threat, contrary to what the Mu'tazilah say. If they say: Did He not say concerning the threat: ﴿The word is not changed with Me, and I am not unjust to the servants﴾ [Qaf: 29]? Thus it is established that the preponderance we have mentioned is correct. And God knows best.

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who avoid the Taghut, not worshipping it, and turn back in repentance to Allah, for them is good news. So give good tidings to My servants, ﴿who listen to the word and follow the best of it. Those are the ones Allah has guided, and those are the people of understanding.﴾ ﴿Is one against whom the word of punishment has been decreed [to be saved]? Would you then save one who is in the Fire?﴾ ﴿But those who feared their Lord will have chambers above them, with chambers built above them, beneath which rivers flow. The promise of Allah; Allah does not fail in His promise.﴾**

Know that when Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned the threat against the worshippers of idols and images, He mentioned the promise for those who avoided worshipping them and guarded themselves against shirk, so that the promise would always be paired with the threat, and thereby the full measure of encouragement and warning would be achieved. In this verse there are several issues.

**The first issue:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari's Qur'an commentary) said: *al-Taghut* is on the pattern *fa'lut*, from *al-tughyan* (transgression), like *al-malakut* (sovereignty) and *al-rahamut* (mercy), except that in it there is a metathesis (*qalb*), by placing the lam before the ayn. In this word there are several kinds of intensification:

First: it is named by the verbal noun, as if the very essence of that thing is transgression.

Second: the form is a form of intensification, for *al-rahamut* is vast mercy, and *al-malakut* is extensive dominion.

Third: what we have mentioned, the placing of the lam before the ayn, and such a form is only resorted to for intensification.

**The second issue:** Scholars differed over whether *al-Taghut* here refers to the Devil (*al-Shaytan*) or to the idols (*al-Awthan*). It was said: it is the Devil. If it is said: they did not worship the Devil; they worshipped the idol. We say: the one who calls to the worship of the idol is the Devil, so that undertaking the worship of the idol is worship of the Devil. It was also said: the intended meaning of *al-Taghut* is the idol, and it was called *tawaghit* (plural) by way of metaphor, because it has no action of its own, and the transgressors (*al-tughat*) are those who worship it; but when transgression occurs at the sight of it and in proximity to it, it was described with this attribute, by naming the effect with the name of the cause according to outward appearance. It was also said: everything that is worshipped and obeyed besides Allah is *taghut*. It is related in the historical accounts that the origin of idol worship was that the people were anthropomorphists (*mushabbiha*), who believed about God that He is a great light, and about the angels that they are lights varying in size; so they set up statues and images in accordance with those imaginings, and they worshipped those statues believing that they were worshipping Allah and the angels.

I say: the sum of the statement in His saying, *"And those who avoid the Taghut"*, meaning: they turned away from worshipping everything other than Allah. His saying, *"and turn back in repentance to Allah"*, meaning: they returned wholly to Allah. I found in the Fifth Book of the *Tawrah* (Torah) that Allah, Exalted is He, said to Moses: "O Moses, respond to your God with all your heart."

I say: as long as there remains in the heart any turning toward other than Allah, one has not responded to one's God with all one's heart. Response with the whole heart is achieved only when the heart turns away from everything other than Allah among the means of acts of obedience. How then can one turn away from them, when one perceives with the senses the causes that lead to effects in this world? We say: the intended meaning of the heart's turning away from them is not that one should judge them to be non-existent, for that is entering into sophistry (*al-sufsata*), which is false. Rather, the intended meaning is that one should know that the Necessary Existent in Himself (*wajib al-wujud li-dhatihi*) is One, and that everything other than Him is possible in its own essence (*mumkin al-wujud li-dhatihi*), and everything that is possible in its own essence exists only through the bringing into being and creating of the Necessary. Then, He, glorified and exalted, has made His bringing things into being of two kinds: some of them occur without intermediary, and these are the world of the heavens and the spiritual beings; and some of them occur through intermediary, and this is the world of the elements and the lower world. When you know things in this manner, you know that all belongs to Allah, from Allah, and through Allah, and that there is no manager except Him and no effective agent other than Him. Then his gaze is detached from these possible things, and his heart remains occupied with the First Effector and the First Originator. For if He has set up the spiritual and physical causes in such a way that they lead to this goal, then this thing comes about; and if He has set them up in such a way that they do not lead to the occurrence of this thing, it does not occur. By this path his gaze is detached from all, and no turning of his heart remains toward anything except the existent

[Page 226]

First. It happened that I was advising some young men about guarding honor and wealth, and he opposed me and said: It is not permissible to rely on effort and striving; rather, one must rely on the decree and destiny of Allah. I said: This is a true word you have heard, but you have not understood its meaning. For there is no doubt that everything is from Allah, Exalted is He, but He, glorified is He, has arranged things in two kinds: some of them He made their occurrence and coming into being dependent on known causes, and others He brings into being without the intermediary of these causes.

As for the first kind: it is the events of this lower world.

As for the second kind: it is the events of that higher world. Once this is established, we say: whoever seeks the events of this lower world not from the causes which Allah, Exalted is He, has determined, that person is contending with Allah in His wisdom and opposing His management; for Allah, Exalted is He, has decreed that these things occur on the basis of those specified and known causes, and you want to obtain them not from those causes. This is the discussion in verifying the turning away from other than Allah and the complete turning toward Allah, Exalted is He. Thus His saying, *"And those who avoid the Taghut"*, is an indication of turning away from other than Allah, and His saying, *"and turn back in repentance to Allah"*, is an indication of wholly turning toward the worship of Allah.

Then, Exalted is He, promised these people several things:

The first of them is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿for them is good news﴾.

Know that this word relates to several aspects:

The first: when does this good news occur? We say: it occurs at the approach of death, when placed in the grave, when standing on the plain of Resurrection, when a group is in Paradise and a group in the Blaze, and when the believers enter Paradise. In each of these standing-places, good news occurs with some kind of goodness, spirit, comfort and fragrant provision.

The second: by what does this good news come about? We say: this good news comes about by the removal of what is disliked and by the attainment of what is desired. As for the removal of what is disliked, His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Fear not, nor grieve﴾ [Fussilat: 30]. Fear is only of the future, and grief is only because of past states. So His saying *"Fear not"* means: do not fear what you will face of the states of the Resurrection, and do not grieve over what has escaped you of the good things of this world. When Allah removed these disliked things from them, He gave them good news of the attainment of goods and felicities, and said: ﴿and rejoice in the Garden﴾ [Fussilat: 30]. He also said in another verse: ﴿On the Day you see the believing men and believing women, their light running before them and on their right: "Good news for you today: gardens beneath which rivers flow"﴾ [al-Hadid: 12]. He also said: ﴿Therein is what the souls desire and what the eyes delight in, and you therein will abide forever﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 71].

The third: who is the bringer of good news? We say: it is possibly the angels, either at death, as in His saying: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death, good, saying: "Peace be upon you"﴾ [al-Nahl: 32], or after entering Paradise, as in His saying: ﴿The angels will enter upon them from every gate: "Peace be upon you, for what you patiently endured; how excellent is the final abode!"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 24]. It is possibly Allah Himself, glorified is He, as He said: ﴿Their greeting on the Day they meet Him will be "Peace"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 44].

Know that His saying, *"for them is good news"*, contains several kinds of emphasis:

First: it implies restriction (*al-hasr*). His saying *"for them is good news"* means: for them and not for others. This indicates that there is no good news for anyone unless he avoids worshipping other than Allah, Exalted is He, and turns wholly toward Allah, Exalted is He.

Second: the definite article in the word *"al-bushra"* (the good news) indicates the reality (*al-mahiyya*), so it indicates that this reality in its entirety belongs to these people, and no share of it remains for others.

Third: there is no difference between information (*al-ikhbar*) and good news (*al-bishara*); good news is the first report of the attainment of goods. Knowing this, we say: all the kinds of reward and good that they heard about in this world, when they hear it at death or in the grave, that is not but information. Thus it is established that this good news is not realized except when information is given of the attainment of other kinds of felicities beyond what they knew and heard of in this world. We ask Allah, Exalted is He, for success in attaining them. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿No soul knows what is hidden for them of the delight of the eyes﴾ [al-Sajda: 17].

Fourth: the one who informs by His saying *"for them is good news"* is Allah, Exalted is He, the Greatest of the great and the most perfect of existents. The condition required for the attainment of this good news is a great condition, namely avoiding what is other than Allah, Exalted is He, and turning wholly toward Allah. When a great sovereign mentions a great condition, then says to one who has fulfilled that great condition: "Rejoice," this good news issuing from the great sovereign, conditioned on the fulfilment of that great condition, indicates that the thing of which the good news is given has reached such a degree of perfection and elevation that minds and thoughts cannot reach its description. Thus it is established that His saying *"for them is good news"* indicates the utmost perfection and felicity in these respects. And Allah knows best.

Know that when He, Exalted is He, said *"for them is good news"*, and this was a general statement, He followed it with a statement which serves as an explanation and elaboration of it, so He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So give good tidings to My servants, who listen to the word and follow the best of it﴾. By "My servants, who listen to the word and follow the best of it," He meant those who avoided and turned back, and no others. This indicates that the head of felicities, the center of goods, and the source of honors is turning away from other than Allah, Exalted is He, and wholly turning toward obedience to Allah. The purpose of this expression is to draw attention to the fact that those who avoided the Taghut and turned back are the ones described as "those who listen to the word and follow the best of it." Thus the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, to draw attention to this point. Some have said: when He, Exalted is He, made clear that those who avoided and turned back have good news, and that this was a high rank which only the foremost attain, and restricting felicity to them implies deprivation for the majority, which does not befit complete mercy, He therefore made the ruling more general, and said: whoever chooses the best in every matter is among the company of the fortunate. Know that this verse indicates several benefits.

* * *

**The first benefit:** the obligation of reflection and reasoning (*al-nazar wa-al-istidlal*). This is because He, Exalted is He, has made clear that guidance and success are linked to a person hearing many things, from which he chooses what is best and most correct. It is known that distinguishing the best and most correct from other things is not attained by hearing alone, because hearing has become a common ground shared by all; for His saying *"who listen to the word"* indicates that hearing is a common quality in which all participate. Thus it is established that distinguishing the best from other things is not achieved by hearing, but is achieved by the proof of reason (*hujjat al-'aql*). This indicates that what necessitates deserving praise and commendation is following the proof of reason, and building the matter upon reflection and reasoning.

**The second benefit:** the paths to establishing the correctness of doctrines and religions are of two kinds:

One of them: establishing the argument and the clear evidence for its soundness by way of acquiring knowledge (*al-tahsil*), and this is something that cannot be attained except by delving into each of the issues in detail.

The second point: before we investigate the proofs, state them, and refute the doubts about them, we present these doctrines and their opposites to our intellects. Whichever doctrine the intellect first judges to be better and more perfect deserves to be accepted more. An example: clear reason testifies that affirming that the God of the world is living, knowing, powerful, forbearing, wise and merciful is better than denying it, so that doctrine is the better one. Likewise, affirming that God Most High does not bring about in His dominion and authority anything except what accords with His will is better than saying that most of what occurs in God's authority is contrary to His will. Also, affirming that God is one, unique, self-sufficient, and free from composition and parts is better than saying He is divisible and composite. Also, saying that He is independent of time and place is better than saying He needs them. Also, saying that God is merciful and generous and may pardon punishment is better than saying that He never pardons it at all. All these matters fall under His saying: ﴿Those who listen to the word and follow the best of it﴾. This is what pertains to choosing the best in matters of belief.

As for what pertains to the matters of obligations (al-takalif), it is of two kinds: some of them are among the acts of worship ('ibadat), and some are among the transactions (mu'amalat). As for acts of worship, an example is our saying: the prayer (salah), in which one says at its opening "Allahu akbar," the intention accompanies the takbir, al-Fatihah is recited in it, tranquility is observed in its five positions, the tashahhud is recited in it, and one exits it by saying "al-salamu 'alaykum." Undoubtedly it is better than a prayer in which none of these conditions is observed, and it obliges the rational person to choose this prayer and leave whatever else there is. The same holds for all the acts of worship.

As for transactions, it is likewise. For example, God Most High legislated retaliation (qisas), blood-money (diyah) and pardon, but He encouraged pardon, saying: ﴿And that you pardon is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237]. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that what is meant by it is a man who sits with a people and hears a discourse containing both good and bad, so he relates the best of what he heard and leaves aside the rest.

Know that God Most High judged those who listen to the word and follow its best by saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom God has guided, and those are the people of understanding﴾. In this there is a wondrous subtlety: the attainment of guidance in the intellect and the spirit is a contingent matter, and it necessarily requires an agent and a recipient. As for the agent, it is God, glorified is He, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom God has guided﴾. As for the recipient, it is indicated by His saying: ﴿and those are the people of understanding﴾, for a person who is not an intellect of complete comprehension cannot have these true cognitions attained in his heart. We have said that the agent of this guidance is God because the substance of the soul, together with the light of intellect that is in it, is receptive to both true belief and false belief. When a thing is receptive to two opposites, its relation to both is equal, and when this is so, it is impossible for that receptive thing to be the cause of the preponderance of one of the two sides. Do you not see that when a body is receptive to motion and rest equally, it is impossible for the very essence of the body to be the cause of the preponderance of one of the two sides over the other? If they say: "We do not say that the essence of the soul and the intellect necessitates this preponderance; rather, we say that it wills to attain one of the two sides, and that volition becomes the cause of that preponderance," we say: this is false, because just as the essence of the soul is receptive to this volition, so too the essence of the intellect is receptive to a volition opposed to that volition. Hence it is impossible for the substance of the soul to be the cause of that volition. Thus it is established that the attainment of guidance necessarily requires an agent and a recipient.

As for the agent: it is impossible that it be the soul itself; rather the agent is God Most High. As for the recipient: it is the substance of the soul. For this reason He said: ﴿Those are the ones whom God has guided, and those are the people of understanding﴾. One does not say: "Is Zayd, do you kill him?" We say: the intended meaning of the heart's turning away from them is not that one should judge them to be non-existent, for that is entering into sophistry (*al-sufsata*), which is false. Rather, the intended meaning is that one should know that the Necessary Existent in Himself (*wajib al-wujud li-dhatihi*) is One, and that everything other than Him is possible in its own essence (*mumkin al-wujud li-dhatihi*), and everything that is possible in its own essence exists only through the bringing into being and creating of the Necessary. Then, He, glorified and exalted, has made His bringing things into being of two kinds: some of them occur without intermediary, and these are the world of the heavens and the spiritual beings; and some of them occur through intermediary, and this is the world of the elements and the lower world. When you know things in this manner, you know that all belongs to Allah, from Allah, and through Allah, and that there is no manager except Him and no effective agent other than Him. Then his gaze is detached from these possible things, and his heart remains occupied with the First Effector and the First Originator. For if He has set up the spiritual and physical causes in such a way that they lead to this goal, then this thing comes about; and if He has set them up in such a way that they do not lead to the occurrence of this thing, it does not occur. By this path his gaze is detached from all, and no turning of his heart remains toward anything except the existent
