Thus, drawing attention to this subtle point becomes a cause for the removal of that grief from the heart of the Messenger (ﷺ). This is the connection (nazm, the coherence of the verse) in the verse. It has also been said: the coherence of the verse is that He, Exalted is He, mentioned another argument establishing that He is the all-knowing God, to show that He is more deserving of worship than these idols.

**The second issue:** The intended meaning of the verse is that He, Exalted is He, takes the souls at death and at sleep. However, He retains the souls for which He has decreed death, and releases the others, which are the sleeping ones, until a specified term, that is, until a time He has set for their death. So His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ means that He takes the souls which He takes at death; He retains them and does not return them to the body. And His saying, ﴿and releases the others until a specified term﴾ means that the soul which He takes during sleep He returns to the body upon waking, and this state remains until a specified term, and that term is the time of death. This is the explanation of the wording of the verse, and it corresponds to the reality. However, it needs further clarification, so we say: The human soul is an expression for a luminous, spiritual substance which, when attached to the body, its light appears in all the limbs, and this is life. We say that at the time of death its attachment is severed from the outward and inward of this body, and that is death. As for the time of sleep, its light is severed from the outward of the body in some respects, but its light is not severed from the inward of the body. Thus it is established that death and sleep are of one genus, except that death is a complete, total severance, while sleep is a partial severance in some respects.

When this is established, it becomes clear that the Powerful, Knowing, Wise One arranged the attachment of the substance of the soul to the body in three modes:

First: that the light of the soul falls upon all parts of the body, outward and inward, and that is wakefulness.

Second: that the light of the soul is withdrawn from the outward of the body in some respects but not from its inward, and that is sleep.

Third: that the light of the soul is completely withdrawn from the body, and that is death. Thus it is established that death and sleep share in each being a taking (tawaffi) of the soul, then one of them is distinguished from the other by specific properties in particular attributes. Such a wondrous arrangement cannot proceed except from the Powerful, Knowing, Wise One, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who give thought.﴾ It is also possible that what is meant by this is that the proof indicates that it is obligatory for the rational person to worship a God described by this power and this wisdom, and not to worship idols, which are inanimate objects having neither perception nor awareness.

Know that the disbelievers raised an objection to this statement. They said: "We do not worship these idols believing that they are gods that harm and benefit. Rather, we worship them only because they are images of persons who were among those brought near to Allah. So we worship them so that those great ones may become intercessors for us with Allah." So Allah answered by saying: ﴿Or have they taken intercessors besides Allah? Say, "Even though they possess nothing and do not reason?"﴾ The statement of the answer is this: these disbelievers will either hope for that intercession from these idols, or from those scholars and ascetics for whom these idols were made as images. The first is false, because these inanimate objects, which are the idols, possess nothing and comprehend nothing, so how can intercession be conceived to come from them?

The second is also false, because on the Day of Resurrection no one possesses anything, and no one can intercede except by the permission of Allah. Thus the true intercessor is Allah, who grants permission for that intercession. Therefore, occupying oneself with His worship is more fitting than occupying oneself with the worship of others. This is what is meant by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say, "To Allah belongs intercession entirely."﴾ Then He explained that there is no dominion for anyone other than Allah, by His saying: ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. Then to Him you will be returned.﴾

Some have held onto His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Say, "To Allah belongs intercession entirely,"﴾ to negate intercession absolutely. This is weak, because we accept that He, glorified is He, if He does not permit intercession, no one can intercede.

If it is said: His saying ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ raises an objection, because this indicates that the one who takes is Allah alone. This is reinforced by His saying: ﴿He who created death and life﴾ [al-Mulk: 2], and by His saying: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258], and by His saying: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah while you were dead and He gave you life﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]. Then Allah, Exalted is He, said in another verse: ﴿Say, "The angel of death will take you"﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11], and He said in a third verse: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him﴾ [al-An'am: 61].

The answer: the one who truly takes is Allah, except that He, Exalted is He, in the world of causes, delegated each kind of action to one of the angels. He delegated the seizing of souls to the angel of death, who is a chief, and beneath him are followers and attendants. So the taking is ascribed in this verse to Allah, Exalted is He, by real ascription, and in the second verse to the angel of death, because he is the chief in this work, and to the rest of the angels, because they are the followers of the angel of death. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 39, verses 45–48:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Allah alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter recoil; but when those other than Him are mentioned, behold, they rejoice.﴾ ﴿Say: "O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You judge between Your servants concerning that over which they used to differ."﴾ ﴿And if those who have wronged had everything on earth and the like of it with it, they would surely offer it as ransom from the terrible punishment on the Day of Resurrection. And there will appear to them from Allah that which they had not been counting upon.﴾ ﴿And there will appear to them the evils of what they earned, and there will descend upon them that which they used to mock.﴾

Know that this is another kind of the ugly deeds of the polytheists: that when you mention Allah alone, saying, "There is no deity except Allah, alone, having no partner," the traces of aversion appear on their faces and in their hearts. And when the idols and images are mentioned, the traces of joy and glad tidings appear in their hearts and breasts. This indicates ignorance and foolishness, because the mention of Allah is the head of all felicities and the title of all goods, whereas the mention of idols, which are base inanimate objects, is the head of all ignorances and foolishness. So their aversion to the mention of Allah alone and their delight in the mention of these idols is among the strongest proofs of gross ignorance and extreme folly. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: "Delight (al-istibshar) and recoil (al-ishmi'zaz) may be contrasted, since each of them is an extreme in its own domain. Delight is that the heart becomes filled with joy until the effect of that joy appears on the surface of the face and it beams. Recoil is that his grief and rage grow great, so the spirit contracts into the inside of the heart, and there remains on the surface of the face the trace of dust and earthly darkness."

When He had related of them this wondrous matter, the falsity of which the innate nature of reason bears witness to, He followed it with two things:

The first of them: He mentioned the great supplication, describing Him first with complete power, which is His saying: ﴿O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, and second with complete knowledge, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. He placed the mention of power before the mention of knowledge because knowledge that He is capable precedes knowledge that He is knowing. When He mentioned this supplication, He said: ﴿You judge between Your servants concerning that over which they used to differ﴾, meaning: their aversion from monotheism and their joy upon hearing polytheism is a matter whose corruption is known by the immediate judgment of reason, and yet these people have persisted in it, so no one can turn them away from this corrupt belief and false creed except You. "From Abu Salamah, who said: I asked Aisha: With what did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to open his prayer at night? She said: He would say: 'O Allah, Lord of Jibril, Mika'il and Israfil, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You judge between Your servants concerning that over which they used to differ. Guide me to the truth in what they have differed about, by Your permission, for indeed You guide whom You will to a straight path.'"

Know that when He, exalted is He, related of them that false creed, He mentioned among their threats several things:

The first of them: that these disbelievers, if they possessed everything on earth of wealth and possessed the like of it along with it, would make the whole of it a ransom for themselves from that severe punishment.

The second of them: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there will appear to them from Allah that which they had not been counting upon﴾, that is: there will appear to them kinds of punishment that were not in their reckoning. Just as the Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning the reward in Paradise: "Therein is that which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no thought has occurred to the heart of a human being," so likewise in punishment a similar thing occurs, namely His saying: ﴿And there will appear to them from Allah that which they had not been counting upon﴾.

The third of them: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there will appear to them the evils of what they earned﴾, and its meaning: there will appear to them the traces of those evil deeds which they had acquired; that is, there will appear to them kinds of punishment that are the traces of those evil deeds which they had acquired. Then He said: ﴿and there will descend upon them﴾ from every direction, ﴿that which they used to mock﴾. By these aspects, exalted is He, He draws attention to the magnitude of their punishment.

[Page 250]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when harm touches man, he calls upon Us; then when We bestow upon him a favour from Us, he says, "I was given it only on [the basis of] knowledge." Rather, it is a trial, but most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿Those before them had said the same, but what they had earned did not avail them.﴾ ﴿So the evils of what they earned befell them. And as for those who wronged among these [people], the evils of what they earned will befall them, and they cannot escape.﴾ ﴿Do they not know that Allah extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it? Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾

Know that this is a description of another of their corrupt ways. When they fall into harm, which is poverty or illness, they turn to Allah, the Exalted, and they hold that the removal of that harm is only from Him. Then, when He bestows upon them a favour, which is either abundance of wealth or health of body, they claim that it was obtained only through their own earning and effort. If it is wealth, they say, "It was obtained through my earning." If it is health, they say, "This was obtained through such-and-such treatment." This is a great contradiction, for in the state of helplessness and need they attributed everything to Allah, and in the state of safety and health they severed it from Allah and ascribed it to their own earning. This is an ugly contradiction. So Allah, the Exalted, made clear the ugliness of their way in what they are upon, both in hardship and in ease, with a concise and eloquent expression. He said: ﴿Rather, it is a trial﴾, meaning: the favour which He bestowed upon this disbeliever is a trial, because when it is obtained gratitude is obligatory, and when it is lost patience is obligatory. Whoever is in this condition is described as a trial, in that the state of the one who is given the favour is tested through him, just as it is said: "I tested the gold with fire," when you expose it to fire in order to know its purity.

* * *

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿But most of them do not know.﴾ The meaning is what we have already mentioned, that this bestowal was only for the sake of testing. Some issues remain in the verse, which we shall mention in the form of questions and answers.

The first question: What is the reason for conjoining this verse with "fa" (then) here, while its counterpart at the beginning of the sura is conjoined with "wa" (and)? The answer: Allah, the Exalted, related before this verse that they recoil from hearing monotheism and rejoice in hearing the mention of partners. Then He mentioned, with the "fa" of sequence, that when they fall into harm and affliction and turn to Allah alone, the first act contradicts the second. This is the benefit of mentioning the "fa" of sequence here. As for the first verse, the purpose is not to show their falling into contradiction at the present time, so ﴿Allah was mentioned﴾ with the letter "wa" and not with the letter "fa."

The second question: What is the meaning of takhwil (bestowal)? The answer: Takhwil is grace (tafaddul); that is, We bestow grace upon him, while he thinks that he found it by right.

The third question: What is meant by His saying: ﴿I was given it only on [the basis of] knowledge﴾? The answer: It may be that the meaning is: "I was given it only on the basis of Allah's knowledge that I deserve it." It may also be that the meaning is: "I was given it only on the basis of my own knowledge that I deserve it." It may also be that the meaning is: "I was given it on a knowledge which, by virtue of that knowledge, I was able to acquire it," such as when he is ill and treats himself, so he says: "I found health only through my knowledge of how to treat myself, and I found wealth only through my knowledge of how to earn."

The fourth question: The favour (ni'mah) is feminine, and the pronoun in His saying ﴿I was given it﴾ refers back to the favour. How then does a masculine pronoun refer back to a feminine noun? Rather, He said after it: ﴿Rather, it is a trial﴾, making the pronoun feminine. What is the reason for this? The answer: The intended sense is: "Until when We bestow upon him something of the favour." The word "favour" is feminine in form, but masculine in meaning, so both usages are permissible.

* * *

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Those before them had said the same, but what they had earned did not avail them﴾. The pronoun in "said" refers to His saying:
[Page 251]
﴿I was given it only on [the basis of] knowledge that is with me﴾, because it is a word or a sentence of what was said. (And "those before them") are Qarun and his people, when he said: ﴿I was given it only on [the basis of] knowledge that is with me﴾, and his people were content with it, so it is as if they said it. It is also permissible that among the earlier nations there were those who said the like of it.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿but what they had earned did not avail them﴾. That is: the false belief and corrupt saying which they acquired did not avail them anything against the punishment of Allah. Rather, ﴿the evils of what they earned befell them﴾. When He had made clear, regarding those earlier people, that the evils of what they had earned befell them, that is, the punishment of their false beliefs and corrupt sayings, He said: ﴿and they cannot escape﴾, that is, they cannot overpower Me in this world or the Hereafter.

* * *

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Do they not know that Allah extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾. He means: Do they not know that Allah, the Exalted, is the One who extends provision to whom He wills at one time and restricts it at another? His saying ﴿and restricts it﴾ means He straitens and constricts. The proof of this is that we see people differing in the abundance and scarcity of provision, and there must be a cause for this. That cause is not a man's intellect or his ignorance, because we see the intelligent and capable man in the greatest straits, and we see the ignorant, ill, and weak man in the greatest abundance. Nor is it because of temperaments, stars, or spheres, because at the hour in which a great kingdom and a dominating sovereign are born, there are also born in that hour a world of humans and a world of animals other than humans, and at that hour a world of plants is also born. When we observe the occurrence of these many things in that single hour, while they differ in happiness and misery, we know that the influence on happiness and misery is not the rising star. When these possibilities are invalidated, we know that the one who influences it is Allah, glorified is He. Through this decisive rational proof, the correctness of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do they not know that Allah extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾ is established.

The poet said:

Neither does Sa'd (the fortunate star) decree by it the buyer (Jupiter),
nor does the ill-omened star Zuhal (Saturn) decree against us.
Rather, it is the judgment of the Lord of the heavens
and the Judge of judges, exalted and majestic.

[Page 250]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when harm touches man, he calls upon Us; then when We bestow upon him a favour from Us, he says, "I was given it only on [the basis of] knowledge." Rather, it is a trial, but most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿Those before them had said the same, but what they had earned did not avail them.﴾ ﴿So the evils of what they earned befell them. And as for those who wronged among these [people], the evils of what they earned will befall them, and they cannot escape.﴾ ﴿Do they not know that Allah extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it? Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾

Know that this is a description of another of their corrupt ways. When they fall into harm, which is poverty or illness, they turn to Allah, the Exalted, and they hold that the removal of that harm is only from Him. Then, when He bestows upon them a favour, which is either abundance of wealth or health of body, they claim that it was obtained only through their own earning and effort. If it is wealth, they say, "It was obtained through my earning." If it is health, they say, "This was obtained through such-and-such treatment." This is a great contradiction, for in the state of helplessness and need they attributed everything to Allah, and in the state of safety and health they severed it from Allah and ascribed it to their own earning. This is an ugly contradiction. So Allah, the Exalted, made clear the ugliness of their way in what they are upon, both in hardship and in ease, with a concise and eloquent expression. He said: ﴿Rather, it is a trial﴾, meaning: the favour which He bestowed upon this disbeliever is a trial, because when it is obtained gratitude is obligatory, and when it is lost patience is obligatory. Whoever is in this condition is described as a trial, in that the state of the one who is given the favour is tested through him, just as it is said: "I tested the gold with fire," when you expose it to fire in order to know its purity.

* * *

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿But most of them do not know.﴾ The meaning is what we have already mentioned, that this bestowal was only for the sake of testing. Some issues remain in the verse, which we shall mention in the form of questions and answers.

The first question: What is the reason for conjoining this verse with "fa" (then) here, while its counterpart at the beginning of the sura is conjoined with "wa" (and)? The answer: Allah, the Exalted, related before this verse that they recoil from hearing monotheism and rejoice in hearing the mention of partners. The second question: What is the meaning of takhwil (bestowal)? The answer: Takhwil is grace (tafaddul); that is, We bestow grace upon him, while he thinks that he found it by right.

The third question: What is meant by His saying: ﴿I was given it only on [the basis of] knowledge﴾? The answer: It may be that the meaning is: "I was given it only on the basis of Allah's knowledge that I deserve it." It may also be that the meaning is: "I was given it only on the basis of my own knowledge that I deserve it." It may also be that the meaning is: "I was given it on a knowledge which, by virtue of that knowledge, I was able to acquire it," such as when he is ill and treats himself, so he says: "I found health only through my knowledge of how to treat myself, and I found wealth only through my knowledge of how to earn."

The fourth question: The favour (ni'mah) is feminine, and the pronoun in His saying ﴿I was given it﴾ refers back to the favour. How then does a masculine pronoun refer back to a feminine noun? Rather, He said after it: ﴿Rather, it is a trial﴾, making the pronoun feminine. What is the reason for this? The answer: The intended sense is: "Until when We bestow upon him something of the favour." The word "favour" is feminine in form, but masculine in meaning, so both usages are permissible.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God. Indeed God forgives all sins. Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes upon you, after which you will not be helped.﴾ ﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive.﴾ ﴿Lest a soul should say: "Alas for my regret over what I neglected concerning God, and indeed I was among the mockers."﴾ ﴿Or lest it say: "If only God had guided me, I would have been among the righteous."﴾ ﴿Or lest it say, when it sees the punishment: "If only I had a return, so that I might be among the good-doers."﴾ ﴿Yes! My signs had already come to you, but you denied them, grew arrogant, and were among the disbelievers.﴾

Know that when He (exalted is He) had extensively spoken of the threat, He followed it with an explanation of the perfection of His mercy, grace and benevolence towards His servants. In this are several issues:

The first issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued with this verse that He (exalted is He) pardons the major sins. They said: We have explained in this book that the usage of the Qur'an is to restrict the word "servants" to the believers. The Almighty said: ﴿And the servants of the All-Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ [al-Furqan: 63], and He said: ﴿A spring from which the servants of God drink﴾ [al-Insan: 6]. And because the word "servants" is mentioned in a context of honour, it must not apply except to the believers. When this is established, it becomes clear that His saying ﴿O My servants﴾ is specific to the believers. Also, the believer is one who acknowledges that he is a servant of God, whereas the polytheists call themselves "servant of al-Lat and al-Uzza" and "servant of the Messiah." Thus it is established that His saying ﴿O My servants﴾ fits only the believers. When this is established, we say: He (exalted is He) said ﴿who have transgressed against themselves﴾, and this is general regarding all transgressors.
* * *
Then the Almighty said: ﴿Indeed God forgives all sins﴾, and this requires that He forgives all sins committed by the believers, and that is the intended meaning. If it is said: This verse cannot be taken according to its apparent meaning, for otherwise it would necessitate the certainty that all sins are forgiven, and you do not say this. So what the verse indicates, you do not hold, and what you hold, this verse does not indicate, so the argument falls. Also, He (exalted is He) said after this verse: ﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes upon you, after which you will not be helped﴾, up to His saying: ﴿suddenly while you do not perceive﴾. Had the meaning of the beginning of the verse been that He had certainly forgiven all sins, He would not have commanded repentance after it, nor would He have warned them of the punishment descending upon them from where they do not perceive. Also, He said: ﴿Lest a soul should say: "Alas for my regret over what I neglected concerning God"﴾. If all sins were forgiven, what need would there be for Him to say: ﴿Lest a soul should say: "Alas for my regret over what I neglected concerning God"﴾? Also, if what was intended were what the apparent wording of the verse indicates, that would be an incitement to sins and a license to commit them, and that is not befitting the wisdom of God. When this is established, it must be interpreted as saying: The intention of it is to alert that it is not permissible for the disobedient person to think that he has no escape from the punishment at all, for whoever believes that is one who despairs of the mercy of God, since none of the disobedient sinners, whenever he repents, has his punishment removed and becomes among the people of forgiveness and mercy. So the meaning of His saying ﴿Indeed God forgives all sins﴾ is: by means of repentance and turning back.

The answer: Your claim that the verse requires that all sins are certainly forgiven, and you do not say this — we say: rather we say this and hold to it. That is because the form ﴿yaghfiru﴾ is the imperfect form, which denotes the future. In our view, God (exalted is He) brings out of the Fire whoever has said: "There is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God." On this assumption, the person with a major sin is certainly forgiven, either before entering the Fire of Hell or after entering it. Thus it is established that what the apparent wording of the verse indicates is exactly our doctrine.

As for your saying: If all sins were entirely forgiven, He would not have commanded repentance — the answer is that in our view repentance is obligatory and the fear of punishment remains, for we do not assert with certainty the complete removal of punishment. Rather we say: perhaps He pardons absolutely, and perhaps He punishes with the Fire for a period and then pardons after that. By this point the answer to the remaining objections is derived. And God knows best.

The second issue: Know that this verse indicates mercy in several respects.

The first: He called the sinner "servant," and servanthood is explained as need, lowliness and poverty, and it befits the Merciful and Generous to bestow goodness and mercy upon the needy, destitute one.

The second: He (exalted is He) attributed them to Himself with the possessive suffix of the first person, saying ﴿O My servants who have transgressed﴾, and the honour of being attributed to Him entails security from punishment.

The third: He (exalted is He) said ﴿who have transgressed against themselves﴾, meaning that the harm of those sins has not returned to Him but rather returns to them. It is sufficient for them, from those sins, that their harms return to them, and there is no need to inflict another harm upon them.

The fourth: He said ﴿do not despair of the mercy of God﴾; He forbade them from despair, so this is a command to hope, and when the Generous commands hope, nothing befits Him but generosity.

The fifth: He (exalted is He) first said ﴿O My servants﴾, and the more fitting would have been to say: "Do not despair of My mercy," but He left this wording and said ﴿the mercy of God﴾, because our saying ﴿God﴾ is the greatest and most exalted of God's names, so the mercy attributed to Him must be the greatest kind of mercy and bounty.

The sixth: When He said ﴿do not despair of the mercy of God﴾, it was necessary that He say: "Indeed He forgives all sins," but He did not say that; rather He repeated the name of God and joined to it the particle "inna" (indeed), which conveys the strongest forms of emphasis, and all of this indicates exaggeration in the promise of mercy.

The seventh: Had He said ﴿He forgives sins﴾, the purpose would have been attained, but He followed it with a word indicating emphasis, saying ﴿all﴾, and this too is among the emphatic devices.

The eighth: He described Himself as ﴿Forgiving﴾, and the word "Forgiving" conveys exaggeration.

The ninth: He described Himself as ﴿Merciful﴾, and mercy carries a benefit beyond forgiveness. So His saying ﴿Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ is an indication of the removal of the causes of punishment, and His saying ﴿the Merciful﴾ is an indication of the securing of the causes of mercy and reward.

The tenth: His saying ﴿Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ conveys restriction, meaning that there is no forgiver and no merciful one except Him, and this conveys perfection in His attribution of forgiveness and mercy (glorified is He). These ten aspects are gathered in this verse, and all of them indicate the perfection of mercy and forgiveness. We ask God Almighty for success through them and for salvation from punishment by His grace and mercy.

* * *
The third issue: They have mentioned several views regarding the occasion of revelation.
It was said: it was revealed concerning the people of Makkah, for they said: "Muhammad claims that whoever worships idols and kills a soul will not be forgiven, and we have worshipped and killed, so how can we submit?"

It was said: it was revealed concerning Wahshi, the slayer of Hamzah, when he wished to embrace Islam but feared that his repentance would not be accepted. When the verse was revealed, he embraced Islam. It was said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Is this for him specifically, or for the Muslims in general?" He said: "Rather, it is for the Muslims in general."

It was said: it was revealed concerning people who had committed grave sins in the Jahiliyyah, and when Islam came they feared that God would not accept their repentance.

It was said: it was revealed concerning 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, al-Walid ibn al-Walid, and a group of Muslims who had embraced Islam and then were tested and fell into trial, and the Muslims used to say about them: "God will not accept their repentance." The fourth issue: Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read ﴿yā ʿibādiya﴾ with a fatha on the ya', and the rest read it without... and 'Asim in some transmissions (without fatha). All of them stop on it with the ya' affirmed, because it is written so in the Mushaf, except in one transmission of Abu Bakr from 'Asim, where he stops without the ya'. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read ﴿taqnitū﴾ with a kasra on the nun, and the rest with a fatha, and both are dialectal forms. * * *
Then the Almighty said: ﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord﴾. The author of al-Kashshaf said: that is, "and repent to Him," ﴿and submit to Him﴾, that is, "and sincerely devote your deeds to Him." He mentioned turning in repentance right after the forgiveness so that no one would hope to obtain it without repentance, and to indicate that it is a necessary condition for it, not obtainable without it. I say: this statement is very weak, for in our view repentance from sins is obligatory, so the command to it entails no criticism of the promise of forgiveness. If they say: If the promise of forgiveness were certainly attained, repentance would not be needed, since repentance is only sought to remove punishment, and when punishment is removed by God's pardon, there is no need for repentance. We say: this is weak, because our doctrine is that although God certainly forgives sins and pardons them with certainty, this pardon and forgiveness occur in two ways: sometimes it occurs from the outset, and sometimes He punishes for a period in the Fire and then brings him out of the Fire and pardons him. The benefit of repentance is the removal of this punishment. Thus it is established that what the author of al-Kashshaf said is weak and has no benefit in it.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God. Indeed God forgives all sins. Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes upon you, after which you will not be helped.﴾ ﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive.﴾ ﴿Lest a soul should say: "Alas for my regret over what I neglected concerning God, and indeed I was among the mockers."﴾ ﴿Or lest it say: "If only God had guided me, I would have been among the righteous."﴾ ﴿Or lest it say, when it sees the punishment: "If only I had a return, so that I might be among the good-doers."﴾ ﴿Yes! My signs had already come to you, but you denied them, grew arrogant, and were among the disbelievers.﴾

Know that when He (exalted is He) had extensively spoken of the threat, He followed it with an explanation of the perfection of His mercy, grace and benevolence towards His servants. In this are several issues:

The first issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued with this verse that He (exalted is He) pardons the major sins. They said: We have explained in this book that the usage of the Qur'an is to restrict the word "servants" to the believers. The Almighty said: ﴿And the servants of the All-Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ [al-Furqan: 63], and He said: ﴿A spring from which the servants of God drink﴾ [al-Insan: 6]. And because the word "servants" is mentioned in a context of honour, it must not apply except to the believers. When this is established, it becomes clear that His saying ﴿O My servants﴾ is specific to the believers. Also, the believer is one who acknowledges that he is a servant of God, whereas the polytheists call themselves "servant of al-Lat and al-Uzza" and "servant of the Messiah." Thus it is established that His saying ﴿O My servants﴾ fits only the believers. When this is established, we say: He (exalted is He) said ﴿who have transgressed against themselves﴾, and this is general regarding all transgressors.
* * *
Then the Almighty said: ﴿Indeed God forgives all sins﴾, and this requires that He forgives all sins committed by the believers, and that is the intended meaning. If it is said: This verse cannot be taken according to its apparent meaning, for otherwise it would necessitate the certainty that all sins are forgiven, and you do not say this. So what the verse indicates, you do not hold, and what you hold, this verse does not indicate, so the argument falls. Also, He (exalted is He) said after this verse: ﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes upon you, after which you will not be helped﴾, up to His saying: ﴿suddenly while you do not perceive﴾. Had the meaning of the beginning of the verse been that He had certainly forgiven all sins, He would not have commanded repentance after it, nor would He have warned them of the punishment descending upon them from where they do not perceive. Also, He said: ﴿Lest a soul should say: "Alas for my regret over what I neglected concerning God"﴾. If all sins were forgiven, what need would there be for Him to say: ﴿Lest a soul should say: "Alas for my regret over what I neglected concerning God"﴾? Also, if what was intended were what the apparent wording of the verse indicates, that would be an incitement to sins and a license to commit them, and that is not befitting the wisdom of God. When this is established, it must be interpreted as saying: The intention of it is to alert that it is not permissible for the disobedient person to think that he has no escape from the punishment at all, for whoever believes that is one who despairs of the mercy of God, since none of the disobedient sinners, whenever he repents, has his punishment removed and becomes among the people of forgiveness and mercy. So the meaning of His saying ﴿Indeed God forgives all sins﴾ is: by means of repentance and turning back.

The answer: Your claim that the verse requires that all sins are certainly forgiven, and you do not say this — we say: rather we say this and hold to it. That is because the form ﴿yaghfiru﴾ is the imperfect form, which denotes the future. In our view, God (exalted is He) brings out of the Fire whoever has said: "There is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God." On this assumption, the person with a major sin is certainly forgiven, either before entering the Fire of Hell or after entering it. Thus it is established that what the apparent wording of the verse indicates is exactly our doctrine.

As for your saying: If all sins were entirely forgiven, He would not have commanded repentance — the answer is that in our view repentance is obligatory and the fear of punishment remains, for we do not assert with certainty the complete removal of punishment. Rather we say: perhaps He pardons absolutely, and perhaps He punishes with the Fire for a period and then pardons after that. By this point the answer to the remaining objections is derived. And God knows best.

The second issue: Know that this verse indicates mercy in several respects.

The first: He called the sinner "servant," and servanthood is explained as need, lowliness and poverty, and it befits the Merciful and Generous to bestow goodness and mercy upon the needy, destitute one.

The second: He (exalted is He) attributed them to Himself with the possessive suffix of the first person, saying ﴿O My servants who have transgressed﴾, and the honour of being attributed to Him entails security from punishment.

The third: He (exalted is He) said ﴿who have transgressed against themselves﴾, meaning that the harm of those sins has not returned to Him but rather returns to them. It is sufficient for them, from those sins, that their harms return to them, and there is no need to inflict another harm upon them.

The fourth: He said ﴿do not despair of the mercy of God﴾; He forbade them from despair, so this is a command to hope, and when the Generous commands hope, nothing befits Him but generosity.

The fifth: He (exalted is He) first said ﴿O My servants﴾, and the more fitting would have been to say: "Do not despair of My mercy," but He left this wording and said ﴿the mercy of God﴾, because our saying ﴿God﴾ is the greatest and most exalted of God's names, so the mercy attributed to Him must be the greatest kind of mercy and bounty.

The sixth: When He said ﴿do not despair of the mercy of God﴾, it was necessary that He say: "Indeed He forgives all sins," but He did not say that; rather He repeated the name of God and joined to it the particle "inna" (indeed), which conveys the strongest forms of emphasis, and all of this indicates exaggeration in the promise of mercy.

The seventh: Had He said ﴿He forgives sins﴾, the purpose would have been attained, but He followed it with a word indicating emphasis, saying ﴿all﴾, and this too is among the emphatic devices.

The eighth: He described Himself as ﴿Forgiving﴾, and the word "Forgiving" conveys exaggeration.

The ninth: He described Himself as ﴿Merciful﴾, and mercy carries a benefit beyond forgiveness. So His saying ﴿Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ is an indication of the removal of the causes of punishment, and His saying ﴿the Merciful﴾ is an indication of the securing of the causes of mercy and reward.

The tenth: His saying ﴿Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ conveys restriction, meaning that there is no forgiver and no merciful one except Him, and this conveys perfection in His attribution of forgiveness and mercy (glorified is He). These ten aspects are gathered in this verse, and all of them indicate the perfection of mercy and forgiveness. We ask God Almighty for success through them and for salvation from punishment by His grace and mercy.

* * *
The third issue: They have mentioned several views regarding the occasion of revelation.

When the verse was revealed, he embraced Islam. It was said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Is this for him specifically, or for the Muslims in general?" He said: "Rather, it is for the Muslims in general."

It was said: it was revealed concerning people who had committed grave sins in the Jahiliyyah, and when Islam came they feared that God would not accept their repentance.

Then He said: ﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾. Know that when He promised forgiveness, He, exalted is He, after this promise commanded several things. The first: He commanded repentance (inābah), which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord﴾. The second: He commanded following the best.

Regarding the meaning of this "best," there are several views:

The first: it is the Qur'an, meaning: follow the Qur'an. The evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book﴾ [az-Zumar: 23].

The second: al-Hasan said: its meaning is: adhere to the obedience of Allah and avoid the disobedience of Allah, for what has been sent down comes in three forms: mention of the ugly so that one may avoid it, mention of the lesser so that one will not desire it, and mention of the best so that one may be strengthened by it and follow it.

The third: the intended "best" is the abrogating (nāsikh) ruling, not the abrogated (mansūkh) one, because the abrogating is better than the abrogated, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or similar to it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106]. And because when Allah, exalted is He, abrogates a ruling and establishes another ruling, our reliance is upon the abrogating one, not the abrogated one.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive﴾. The purpose of this is threat and warning, and the meaning is that the punishment will come upon them unexpectedly while they are heedless of it. Know that when He, exalted is He, warned them of the punishment, He explained what they would say should the punishment descend upon them. Allah, exalted is He, related from them three kinds of utterances. The first is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿lest a soul should say, "Oh, my regret over what I neglected concerning Allah, and indeed I was among the mockers"﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿lest a soul should say﴾ is an object of purpose, i.e., out of dislike that a soul should say: ﴿lest a soul should say, "Oh, my regret over what I neglected concerning Allah"﴾. As for the indefinite form of the word "soul" (nafs), there are two views. The first: it is permissible that a particular soul distinguished from the rest of souls is intended, due to its being singled out for greater harm, which does not negate its desire for sins. The second: it is permissible that it is intended to denote plurality, because it is established in the science of the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh) that a ruling mentioned immediately after a descriptor appropriate to it indicates a probable inference that the ruling is caused (muʿallal) by that descriptor. So His saying ﴿Oh, my regret (ḥasratā)﴾ indicates the utmost sorrow and the extreme of grief, and it is mentioned immediately after His saying, exalted is He: ﴿over what I neglected concerning Allah﴾. Neglect in obedience to Allah, exalted is He, is appropriate to the intensity of regret, and this requires that this regret occurs at the occurrence of this neglect, and that indicates generality by this route.

The second issue: Those who affirm body parts for Allah, exalted is He, argued for affirming the "side" (janb) from this verse. Know that our proofs against body parts for Allah are abundant, so there is no benefit in repetition. We say: even assuming that the intended "janb" is a specific organ of Allah, exalted is He, it is impossible for neglect to occur in it, and so it is established that one must resort to interpretation (taʾwīl). The exegetes have various expressions about it. Ibn ʿAbbās said: he means, "I neglected from the reward of Allah." Muqātil said: "I neglected from the remembrance of Allah." Mujāhid said: "in the command of Allah." al-Hasan said: "in the obedience of Allah." Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: "in the right of Allah." Know that multiplying these expressions does not bring relief to the breast nor cure the thirst, so we say: the "janb" is called janb because it is one of the sides of that thing, and a thing that is among the necessary attributes and consequences of a thing is as if it were one of its troops and one of its sides. When this resemblance arose between the "janb" which is the organ and that which is necessary for and follows a thing, it is for this reason that the word "janb" came to be used appropriately for truth, command and obedience. The poet said:

Do you not fear Allah regarding one who loves you (janb wāmiq), for whom a heart burns with longing for you and is torn apart?
